subtopic: MR. HOWARD    BRIEFS TO ROYAL COMMISSION ON BICULTURALISM
MR. HOWARD    BRIEFS TO ROYAL COMMISSION ON BICULTURALISM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege involves the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism. May I preface my question by quoting from the order in council establishing the commission as follows:
-to inquire into and report upon the existing state of bilingualism and biculturalism in Canada and to recommend what steps should be taken to develop the Canadian confederation on the basis of an equal partnership between the two founding races-
This is the important part.
-taking into account the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada-
And so on. I have just received this morning a document from the royal commission. It is a memorandum regarding the procedure to be followed in hearings before the commission. On page 2, under the heading of "nature of briefs", part (e) reads as follows:
Briefs must be written in either French or English, or in the two languages, according to the preference of the persons who submit them.
It is my contention that it is not possible to take into account the contribution made by the other ethnic groups to the cultural enrichment of Canada by so restricting the language in which briefs must be written for presentation to the commission. Accordingly, founded on my question of privilege I move:
That this house declares, notwithstanding anything to the contrary, that briefs to the royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism may be written and presented in any language.
My motion is seconded by the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott).

subtopic: MR. HOWARD    BRIEFS TO ROYAL COMMISSION ON BICULTURALISM
speechtext:
May I ask if there is any hon. member who would like to speak to this question of privilege before I try to give a decision. If not, then I may say that questions of privilege are extremely important matters. The Speaker has to be convinced that there is a prima facie case. This is one of the elements. In the present circumstances I do not believe there is a prima facie case for a question of privilege. It is rather in the nature of a complaint. Having had an opportunity of studying this motion I And that 28902-5-237
it does not take on the character of a substantive motion. I regretfully must come to the conclusion that in my opinion there is no question of privilege.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Caron for concurrence in the second report of the standing committee on privileges and elections, and on the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Question.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I would like to say a few words about the amendment under discussion at the present time. I realize that nothing I might say will change much for at this stage questions are pretty well settled. I say this openly and publicly, because it reflects my firm belief, and probably that of the public as well.
Mr. Speaker, before coming to the heart of the matter and speaking to the amendment of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I wish to say that I apologize for my fellow French Canadians who, yesterday, have shown to the nation what stuff they are made of.
Actually, Mr. Speaker, I feel that yesterday you got in this house a fair sample of the political views of some French Canadians.
This day will remain forever in the annals of parliament as a typically bitter fight between French Canadians which simply made me sick.
I think we could blame the Speaker for not having put a stop with a firm hand to this brotherly slaughter, because he allowed some members to stray completely from the subject.
But, on the other hand, I think that the Speaker deserves to be thanked, because he wanted to give us a sample of what some of our fellow French Canadians can do and say. I shall never forget it as long as I live.
Mr. Speaker, I disagree with the conclusions of the committee on privileges and elections because its members have not dealt with the case in point. You should be mindful of the fact that the committee was asked simply to reach a decision as to the recognition of the party. Yet, sidetracking the issue


completely, the committee set themselves to the task of determining the order of precedence of the various opposition parties in this house, which was precisely the task assigned to the Speaker, following the conclusions reached in the committee's report on the recognition of the different opposition parties.
And as a final conclusion to its work, the committee is asking counsel to settle the one and only question on which the committee was supposed to make a decision.
Mr. Speaker, I suspect the members of the committee on privileges and elections were badly informed. And to substantiate that impression, I submit that the most important piece of evidence in the matter was almost intentionally put aside. I refer to the statement signed by the 12 members who are giving their support to the new leader in this house, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), and repudiating the former one, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson).
Great efforts were made at all the meetings of the committee to produce a letter from our present leader in the house, the hon. member for Villeneuve, in which he was just stating the results of the various steps taken by the 13 members since the Granby convention.
The hon. member for Lapointe, the only representative of our party on the committee-whereas the party of the hon. member for Red Deer had two representatives, although it has fewer members than our group-did try to produce that essential proof, but he had great difficulty-in fact he was nearly prevented from giving evidence by the committee chairman himself-to say anything about it.
We suspect that everything was done so that the situation would not be clarified before the committee. That is why it is our duty to say to the house what really happened, so that all those present may still believe in the rights of the members in this chamber and judge the matter impartially.
Mr. Speaker, I read with great attention the minutes of proceedings and the evidence given to the committee on privileges and elections. I did not attend regularly the proceedings of the committee, except for five or six minutes at a time. When I saw the absurdity of these proceedings, I left in a hurry.
There are some good points, some less good and some bad in these reports of the committee on privileges and elections. After sifting all its verbosity, and leaving out all the unnecessary words and evidence, there remain three facts that may serve my argumentation.

I want to speak of the basic argumentation held by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I shall use also the evidence, given by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe), to refute the proposal made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) in conjunction with the Liberal members.
All day yesterday there was mention of the legal rights of the parties. Some petty French Canadians even cried in the house that it was our duty not to grant the rights and privileges our group is entitled to because that was against the law. Well, let those people show us beyond any doubt that legally third parties do not exist in the British parliamentary procedure. The whole matter is definitely based on that point.
Mr. Speaker, if one reads carefully the statements and information, especially the one presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, as well as the other statements, one realizes how ridiculous is that petty political fight, which I shall denounce throughout the province.
They say that as a group we are not entitled to our privileges. Well, Mr. Speaker, if that is not filibustering or the worst kind of muzzling ever seen in this parliament, I wonder what it is.
What did the hon. member for Labelle say, he who claims to be the champion of the rights and laws of parliament? On page 24 of the same report he is quoted as saying:
As Mr. Girouard said, there are in the constitution, in the British North America Act, or in law no precedents anywhere which lay down criteria, standards, definitions and conditions as regards parties.
When the hon. member for Labelle claims that there is nothing to determine that and then pretends to defend the law and legal principles here, I wonder on what kind of an argument he can base such an idiotic statement as the one he made to the committee.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre goes on:
Parties are national organizations formed by Canadian citizens. They do not exist in the House of Commons. They exist in the House of Commons as members of parliament, as groups.
And not as a party. Such is the law. Those who try to evade the law do so to play politics. But to promote justice, one must comply with the law and this is the last point I wish to make today.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre continues:
I suggest that the most dangerous thing we could do would be for the House of Commons by a ma.iority vote to decide that parties A. B and C are official parties in Canada and parties D, E and F are not.

Privileges and Elections
That is just what you did, and what you are doing now; you want another party to decide what only your party has the right to determine.
And the member for Winnipeg North Centre says:
No need for me to quote historical examples for that kind of thing.
Then, he pursues his argument by saying, as you may see on that same page 24 of the report:
The group supporting Mr. Caouette is actually asking the House of Commons to take a decision as to who of the two is the party leader.
Please note that in the request of the hon. member for Villeneuve, the latter addresses himself to Mr. Speaker, advising him of the fact that we are a group, and asking him to be so kind as to recognize us, which is the object of his letter.
And the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre adds:
In internal matters-
If the Conservative party asked the House of Commons to decide who is the leader, Mr. Diefen-baker or Mr. X, or if the Liberals or ourselves asked such question, we would be told that it is none of our business-
The internal business of Social Credit has been explained to us. It is not up to us to take any decision in this matter. It is not for us to decide whether a federal Canadian party is official or not.
It seems to me that we have here a rather clear interpretation of the law, so that each hon. member may intelligently and, more particularly, legally decide for himself.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also said:
We have to decide, on the evidence, how many groups or members there are in the house and then, having made a decision on that, we will have to decide on the recommendations to be made to the Speaker concerning the precedence of each group and the seating arrangement.
Although there are no citations supporting the contention that parties exist in the House of Commons on any official basis, there are a couple of citations that support the fact that we are various groups. I have here a citation from Beauchesne which, I hope, Mr. Beauchesne will let me read in one of the official languages of the country.
In section 20, page 17 of Beauchesne, fourth edition, there is a judgment which was made a long time ago, and in order to tell the whole story I had better read it. He says:
The members who do not support the government and do not belong to the opposition party should all be considered as Independents.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it is the very crux of the matter. A thorough examination of the rules and regulations allow one to realize that, actually, there are only in this house two official groups which can really be called parties, that is to say the party in office and the official opposition. The other so-called parties are merely groups which are reconized through the courtesies of parliament. That is how we should really interpret our rules and regulations.

Privileges and Elections
It is all very well to fool around with the term "party", but actually, one may only speak of a third party by extending the courtesies of this house to the second, third and fourth opposition groups. It is a question of courtesy, and nothing more.
That is why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) added:
When I first came to the House of Commons, Mr. King used to quote this often and he was very reluctant to grant to the C.C.F. and Social Credit parties of that day the courtesies which he granted them later on. Even Mr. Beauchesne had to admit certain facts... I think... we have to decide... but, let us not commit the folly of deciding by a majority vote of the members, which are official parties and which are not.
In regard to what constitutes a party, I believe, in view of the interpretation of the English law, that there is no use for the three minor groups, on this side, to use the word party as a legal word; it is extended to them only as a matter of courtesy.
This is the reason why I was saying a while ago that the main argument that could be raised is that if the Liberal party, if all the Liberal members, had stopped playing politics in order to treat this situation strictly from a legal point of view I really believe that they would not have been so hasty in reaching a decision.
Mr. Speaker, the second point to which I would like to draw the attention of the house is a statement by the member for Cariboo (Mr. Leboe). The hon. member upheld the theory in regard to the protection of the electorate. The member for Cariboo said, as shown on page 34 of the same committee report:

I think we here must protect our electorate in regard to anything we have before us.

A little further he added:
1Text]
The rights and privileges of the electorate must be protected.

If we want to protect the rights and privileges of the electorate I wonder whether we should not start by protecting the rights and privileges of those whom this same electorate has chosen. My electors voted for Social Credit, through the Ralliement du Credit social. I owe it to myself to respect the views of my electors. I am convinced that my electors would never have forgiven me, after I was elected under the label of the Raillie-ment du Credit social or the Social Credit, if I had associated with the Liberals in the house in order to form a compact entity.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote part of the resolution submitted by a Liberal member; that resolution does not stand up

once it is explained, but I should like to quote a brief passage of what was said by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner). He stated, as found on page 36 of the same report:
Mr. Chairman, I will follow the example of Mr. Drouin, if I might, who said that we are acting here as a jury.
That is quite an interesting little passage because the committee claims for itself the role of a jury.
If you wish, Mr. Speaker, let us find out together how a committee can be officially considered to be a court of inquiry when it does not carry its assignment further. If it is to be a jury, as suggested by Mr. Drouin, first of all it should have at least the basic attribute of a tribunal made up of a jury and a presiding officer. All members of the jury should meet certain essential conditions such as integrity and the absence of any family or political ties with the accused.
Above all, the jury should not be at the same time prosecutor and judge. I am asking myself whether this committee, this little tribunal, is not fundamentally wrong? I still wonder whether the majority of members of this committee do not have preconceived ideas, whether they have not prejudged the case? Why have they strayed from the right road throughout the whole inquiry and then, out of breath, decided to pass the burden to somebody else?
I believe that those who have voted for us in that committee were those whose sole purpose was to unearth truth, so that justice might prevail. And I thank them from the bottom of my heart for, though few details were available to them, they have succeeded in unearthing the truth.
Are you led into that frantic dance of lost pains by your national conscience or by fear of the electorate?
Who is acting most ridiculously in this hullabaloo? Well, take a good look at yourselves, gentlemen. You are merely the shadow of yourselves and the people who elected you to represent them here will never forgive you your political dictatorship.
If we consider the political status-

Privileges and Elections Liberals, provided the present government refuses the right to speak to the only French Canadian group legally representing the French Canadian voters in this house. It is disgusting, but that is what that group has given evidence of, by systematically uniting with the others to muzzle us.
Mr. Speaker, I ask of all those who consider the small trips which were granted to our fellow citizens, I am of the opinion that this is too high a price for a few moments of glory.
Mr. Speaker, I ask of all those who consider justice above their partisanship to have a human thought.
You, former creditistes, have always been told that in the Social Credit party, principles should rank higher than people. The first of those principles is that a true creditiste holds that his very first responsibility is to the people who have elected him.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, I have nothing against-

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is the Ralliement.

subtopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, it is the Ralliement not Social Credit that got you elected, and that is what we have been trying to have you understand, but it seems that as far as the hon. member for Labelle is concerned, that is impossible.
Mr. Speaker, I do not bear any grudge against the hon. member for Red Deer. He is an excellent man, a nice guy as we say back home. In fact, he is such a nice guy that he gives himself and ourselves to everyone.
I have to reprove seriously my fellow citizens. We have been fighting for the recognition of the French fact for months. Looking at certain French Canadian jokers who take pleasure in knocking their brothers because they were bold enough to demand their right to speak, I am sometimes ashamed of my race.
Mr. Speaker, we have been lowered to that level by politickers who have always used us. And to think that they are ready to revise our constitution. What a bunch of jokers. They should go and hide elsewhere to perpetrate their contemptible actions. They should no longer profane this house by their servility. As a French Canadian fellow citizen I say to them: return to your water-carrying chores. It is not with people of their kind that we will have a bilingual country, a constitution which will guarantee the rights of the two great races, and that we will succeed in shaping a strong Canada based on two great cultures.
And, in order to be fair to everybody, I now want to commend not only those who voted, but those who had the courage not to vote in order to prevent one of their

French Canadian fellow citizens from speaking in this house. I commend them for having had this courage as I shall blame those who had the cheek, under the pretext of an inexist-ing law, to deprive a group of fellow citizens of their right of speech in the house.
It would certainly be of interest to the house to know what the committee could not know.
We are a political party-and when I say political party, I always mean it in a legal sense, and not the way other opposing parties see it: a political party by courtesy- because we were elected as Social Credit members through the Ralliement des creditistes, which is a provincial organization interested in federal politics. As a matter of fact, this is the case for each of the provinces, and the Alberta and British Columbia groups are no exception, because their members were also elected by their respective provincial organizations. To the contrary of other parties, with us, it is the provincial organizations which see to the election of their members. Each provincial organization is autonomous. That is why those younger Social Crediters who say that they have been elected through the Ralliement des creditistes are completely mistaken.
In short our federal party is a national party comprising all provincial organizations, as it has always been maintained throughout Canada with regard to the two ethnical groups.
It is somewhat difficult for members of the old parties who have experienced only the melting pot to understand. Someone will say:	but there was a split. Well, that,
again, is true. It happened after a legally convened meeting at the Granby convention, on the unanimous recommendation of nearly 1,500 delegates, when we had 19 members from Quebec who had been elected through the Ralliement des creditistes. I want to stress that the reasons for our acting in this way are connected with the administration of our party, and I do not care to discuss those reasons here, as some hon. members did yesterday. Those reasons are, as I say, of an internal nature. We acted legally and that is why we are asking Mr. Speaker to do what he has to do when there is a majority vote.
We found, to our regret, that we had to depose our former parliamentary leader, and I repeat "former parliamentary leader" because our opponents are always playing on the words "national leader" and "parliamentary leader". We had to depose our parliamentary leader in order to replace him by a new one, the hon. member for Villeneuve.
Please note that I do not question the right of the hon. member for Red Deer to

affiliate himself with another party, but when he makes commitments on behalf of the whole party, then I cannot go along with him. And I say to him, in a quite friendly spirit, as
I	say to those French Canadians whose confidence and respect he has kept: Stop that game, stop trying to usurp other people's property. After all, it is our group, the group from Quebec, which has created the present Social Credit movement.
We say: "Go on, but leave us our clothes." You see, we do not ask much, leave us our rights as a group.
You have more to do to find someone to your own image and likeness. Why not cross to the other side of the house; go back to your Liberal brothers. The chance of survival for your group is on the other side, although it will cause some small inconvenience to those who will accept you, because some are so much tinted in blue that they will stand out a little.
We feel no bitterness against anyone and we want only one thing: that each member enjoy fully his rights and privileges as concerns his group.
You recognized the rights of the group of
II	and you refuse the same rights to a group of 13, therefore a majority group.
All responsible papers shout fallacy and injustice. Throughout its history, Canada has never witnessed such a gag being imposed on a group of French Canadians in this parliament by a Liberal government. For us, we shall never-and please pay attention to those words-we shall never dare deprive another group of its rights to speak in this house.
Through the doubtful doings of the committee, under cover, to hide the truth to which several still sincere members of that committee were entitled, a purely political purpose was achieved, that of killing a potential political enemy. In fact, for the old parties, the member for Red Deer represents no danger at all, but the member for Villeneuve is a man to beat. I doubt that the Liberals have been deceived, and that, you know it very well. The battle is fought for that sole purpose.
I claim that this ridiculous situation has lasted too long already, as shown by your behaviour in the house. We might think this is a perfect Babel.
One day you vote for one thing, the other day, you vote precisely for the contrary. In this house, a strong majority vote imposes a gag on us, so as to stop us from speaking, to deny our political party the right to its privileges, and, two days later, in this same house, remorsefully, a unanimous vote restores to us the rights which had been so arbitrarily
Privileges and Elections taken away. Through partisanship, you vote for a blatant injustice. But the next day, fearing public opinion, which shows its disgust in all the newspapers, as well as over the radio and on television, you are forced to back down.
They give the impression that Canada suffers from paralysis.
It is not by shouting at the top of their voice "I am a French Canadian, I am of French Canadian descent", that they will be useful to their race but rather by working in close co-operation with their brothers.
It is not by using the whip on their brothers that they will become great Canadians. It is rather by taking all the means at their disposal to defend them, in spite of their faults and whatever their party.
It is not over the dead body of their brother, knocked down without pity, that they will be able to proclaim themselves the champions of French Canada, but rather by fighting unswervingly and legally beside him until victory is achieved.

Mr. Speaker, I can hear my learned friend opposite, and that reminds me of the little Chicago of 1946-48, whose job it was to always interrupt those who had the floor. It is a contest to find out who can utter the greatest nonsense. Those characters are holding such a competition to prevent members of the house from speaking.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I say that we are of our times and we wish to take a stand, in this chamber, for the small nations of the world, and that in the name of democracy and the rights of man, the right of all people, as well as all groups and individuals, to be free.
What do we say about Russia, for instance, which does not recognize the existence of small parties? We do not want communism. We do not want a Cuban-type organization. We do not want Castroism in Canada. Are not the Liberals acting toward us now exactly like that good man Khrushchev is doing in Russia and Castro is doing in Cuba? So much so that last night I told newspapermen: "I think it is becoming more and more obvious: red is as red in Moscow as it is in Ottawa and red is as red in Ottawa as it is in Moscow." That is the situation we find ourselves in when we are subjected to a kind of treatment like the one we now have to put up with in the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) are in the house at present. I regret the absence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) but I urge the federal leaders to remember the present position of their party and to stop telling hon. members, through their whip, how they should vote.

Let there be a free vote in the house to determine whether or not we care for democratic principles and whether or not in Canada men have the right to associate and to look after their own affairs. Let us recognize today man's right to form a party and be acknowledged as such. By doing that, the Liberals would be better accepted in Canada and all hon. members would have the respect of the Canadian electorate but, above everything else, they would command the respect of democracies throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he can bring the house up to date on any communications between the government and
Inquiries of the Ministry the President and secretary of labour of the United States in connection with the trusteeship legislation. Also, is the government aware of the fact, as I suggested when I spoke in the house on October 1, that if this legislation is proceeded with there is danger of a mass walkout of the S.I.U. workers? Furthermore, is the government aware of the threats made by the S.I.U., both in Montreal and Vancouver, to march on Ottawa by way of protest which, of course, will mean the holding up of shipping in those two ports?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRUSTEESHIP LEGISLATION
subsubtopic: THREATENED MARCH ON OTTAWA BY S.I.U.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope I will be able to deal with all the right hon. gentleman's questions, which are very important and of immediate urgency. The first question he asked, perhaps not the first but the one I have in my mind at the moment, was whether the government was aware of the danger that might be caused by the putting into effect of the government trusteeship legislation in view of the possibility of certain unions, or one union and the members of that union, taking exception to that legislation and attempting to destroy its effect. The government is very much aware of that danger, Mr. Speaker, and has been for some time. The danger would have been even greater if we had acted precipitously last July before we had attempted to bring about a private trusteeship.
The right hon. gentleman also asked whether I was aware of the development that had been reported today, namely a possible march on Ottawa by members of the S.I.U., and the action reported by their leaders in calling the seamen away from work and holding up shipping in that way. I have seen these reports, which must arouse not only great interest but great concern on the part of all members of the house and indeed of the country as a whole. The call to strike, if that is the right expression, and if it is not a strike it is a threatened strike, seems to have been issued in a bulletin called "Instruction Bulletin No. 1." I received this bulletin just before lunch. It is issued to members of the seamen's union by what is referred to as the seamen's rights committee of the seafarers international union of Canada. The instructions seem to be based on the assumption that the trusteeship law is in effect.
This, Mr. Speaker, of course is not the case. The law has passed all the stages of discussion in this house and has been approved by the Senate. It has not yet received royal assent, though I expect it will receive royal assent this afternoon. It will then not be in effect until it is proclaimed by the government. Although the law is not yet in effect, the

Inquiries of the Ministry government certainly does not intend to defer action in this regard because of the pressure that might be exerted on it, or attempted, by a strike or the threat of a strike. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, under certain circumstances that pressure would have the opposite effect.
I think the action called for by these instructions contained in bulletin No. 1 issued by this committee is especially to be condemned at this particular time when negotiations for a private settlement, and one that would be satisfactory to the Canadian government and the Canadian Labour Congress, have been resumed. They were resumed last Saturday and they give hope-I can certainly go that far-of an early and successful conclusion. To have this action taken by the union concerned when so much progress has been made in these resumed negotiations for a private settlement which would be satisfactory to both sides of the line and to the labour union organizations concerned, I think is a deplorable development. Certainly this kind of threat does not in any way facilitate these negotiations.
We are in touch with the United States at the government level, and I understand the union organizations are in touch with each other. I do not need to tell the house how difficult and delicate these negotiations are. I do not want to say anything at this time which would interfere in any way with a very early and successful conclusion.

I should like to ask a further question. In these discussions that are taking place, I take it at government level, is the United States insisting that on this trustee board there shall be United States labour representation? Is that the condition upon which the question will be determined as to whether or not a private arrangement can be concluded?
I should like also to ask the Prime Minister, since he has gone into quite a bit of detail, does he think that having legislation passed by both houses of parliament and negotiations thereafter has a weakening effect on the authority of parliament to pass this legislation? There still has to be royal assent given, but when royal assent is given does the government intend to proclaim the legislation, or simply to use it as a means of pressure to gain a trusteeship settlement that apparently is being considered at the moment?

subtopic: TRUSTEESHIP LEGISLATION

the determining voice in any board of trustees would have to be Canadian. There is no doubt about that.
I want to assure the right hon. gentleman we are proceeding in the normal way with our legislation. I understand that royal assent will be given to it this afternoon. If within the next day or two or over the week end there is an assurance of a satisfactory private trusteeship, the act will not be proclaimed until that assurance is removed. However, we are not going to suspend the operation of this act for long during these negotiations. I hope we will reach a successful conclusion within the next day or two. If that is possible, and I think it is possible, then surely it would be a great mistake to proclaim this act tomorrow.

subtopic: REFUSAL BY U.S. TO ADMIT CHINESE CANADIAN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REFUSAL BY U.S. TO ADMIT CHINESE CANADIAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister, of which I have sent him notice. Is the government aware of the case of Mr. Wayson S. Choy, a Canadian born citizen who was refused admission to the United States on the ground that half his ancestry was Chinese; and will the government make representations to the government of the United States that such discrimination is inconsistent with the universal declaration of human rights, and offensive to Canadians?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REFUSAL BY U.S. TO ADMIT CHINESE CANADIAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my hon. friend for having given me notice of this question and also for having given me a little time to do the research which was required to get the information. I am answering him at some length because I know there are some questions of principle involved in his question. This matter was brought to my attention by Mr. Choy and others, and in view of the interest that it has aroused in the house and in other parts of Canada I would like to explain it.
At the outset I should like to make it very clear that as for Canadian law and policy, the present government, like its predecessor, is firmly opposed in principle and in practice to racial discrimination. Mr. Choy may rest assured that as far as Canadian law and policy are concerned, his Canadian citizenship is the same as that of every other Canadian born citizen.
With respect to the United States law relating to immigrant visas-and this is the matter immediately under discussion-it has since 1924, with some exceptions, been based on a national origins system. There are quotas, however, based on country of birth for most countries of the world. A separate- and this is the exception-and very small quota, based on ancestry and not place of birth, was provided for persons whose ancestry lies in what that law calls the "Asia-Pacific triangle". If persons born in Canada and Latin America fall within the rules relating to ancestry in the Asia-Pacific triangle, they come under this particular quota.
The result of this law in Mr. Choy's case was that when he applied to the United States consul for an immigrant visa in order to work in the United States, he was told that his application could be considered only under the Chinese quota, which is filled for several years ahead. Mr. Choy considered that the effect of the United States law is to discriminate on racial grounds, in the

matter of immigration visas, against him and a particular category of Canadian born citizens.
While it may not be appropriate, Mr. Speaker, for the Canadian government to make official and formal representations to the United States government against the racial origins features of United States domestic immigration law, this does not mean that the Canadian government favours the inclusion of racial origin provisions in the immigration laws of the United States or any other country. These provisions, however, are not directed against Canada. A prospective immigrant of Chinese ancestry would find himself up against the Asia-Pacific quota provisions regardless of what country he was born in.
An additional reason, Mr. Speaker, for not making formal representations to the United States government is the fact that on July 23 of this year President Kennedy sent a message to congress proposing important changes in the quota system. He described the national origins system as "an anachronism, for it discriminates among applicants for admission into the United States on the basis of accident of birth". He specifically proposed the repeal of the Asia-Pacific ancestry formula, which is the part of the law that affects Mr. Choy. The President's proposals are now being considered in congress.

subtopic: REFUSAL BY U.S. TO ADMIT CHINESE CANADIAN
speechtext: A supplementary question. Does the Prime Minister not feel that it might aid the President if the view of the Canadian government on this matter, which I suggest is more than just a domestic matter, were conveyed formally, rather than unofficially, to the United States government?

subtopic: REFUSAL BY U.S. TO ADMIT CHINESE CANADIAN

subsubtopic: WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he is now ready to make the statement that he was going to make on Wednesday about the extension of the winter works program for the city of Toronto.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION OF WINTER
subsubtopic: WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to make this statement yesterday, but as my hon. friend knows there was not much opportunity for statements on orders of the day yesterday. But I am glad to reply to him now.
As the Minister of Labour stated in this house on June 10, the municipal winter works incentive program for 1963-64 will operate from November 1, 1963 to April 30, 1964, inclusive. It has been found that under the seven and one half month period during which the program was in effect in recent years, many municipalities commenced their projects in the fall, discontinued work during the real winter months, and resumed construction in the spring. This, of course, defeated the purpose of the program to a considerable extent. The objective, as hon. members know, is to have municipalities carry their projects through the winter months when seasonal unemployment is at its highest.
The effective period of the program already announced for next winter covers six months of the year, which should permit municipalities to do some preliminary work in the

fall and carry projects through to completion during the month of April.
A number of representations have been received regarding the effective period of the program for the coming winter, but it is not the intention to extend the period of the program beyond the six months, November 1 to April 30.

speechtext: I cannot allow that to pass-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: It seems to me that attacks of the character that have been made are insufferable, and should not be allowed to continue. Merely because there are certain members who do not seem-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am speaking to a question of privilege, and surely I am going to be heard to the end of my question of privilege without interruption.

I suggest, sir, that we observe the rules in this house, and when an hon. member raises a point of order we allow the Chair to decide whether or not there is a point of order, and not call into question the hon. member's right to raise it.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

The Secretary of State has seen fit to draw the attention of the Chair to the fact that, on a number of occasions recently, I have raised points of order in respect of the Secretary of State. Once again I would call the attention of the Chair to the fact that he raised this particular point of order and then changed it to a question of privilege. He did so without recognition of the Chair. I should like also to call attention to the fact that a few moments ago, when the question period was finished, the Secretary of State rose without the consent of the Chair in order to tell what he thought was a funny joke. On that occasion Your Honour saw fit to ask him to return to his seat. The Chair has asked the Secretary of State once today to resume his seat, and only a few days ago on a similar point of order he was requested to return to his seat.
Now he has raised a point of order which he has changed to a question of privilege. Again, I state that no one in this house has violated Your Honour's rulings as often as the Secretary of State.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Perhaps this is the time to give a short explanation of how I believe the Chair should act. It is this: Under our system of government and under the rules of the house, we recognize first of all the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), then the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), who has a very official position under our system; then members of the cabinet; then members of the front bench and I should, of course, include there the leaders of the various parties; then, from there we do the best we can.
Now, it is true that the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) carries that title, but he is also the house leader and of necessity must
Privileges and Elections be on his feet more frequently than most members. He has to conduct the business of the house. He is responsible for a great deal of its planning. I am not aware, at least not consciously aware, of any time when he has broken any rule that I have tried to establish in this house. Every time he rose, and he must rise very frequently, I thought in order to save the time of the house I did not have to call, "The Hon. Secretary of State". I always catch his eye or he waits his turn. Hon. members will appreciate that custom dictates that the front benches are considered first, and are given an opportunity to speak first. Then, we gradually work back.
I think if that is understood hon. members, no matter where they sit, will realize they all are given a reasonable opportunity. In so far as I am concerned, I am elected by all of the members and not by a government, a party or a group. So far as I am concerned, all members are equal and have the same rights.

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: On that point, is this why the Chair-

maintopic: MOTION FOR CONCURRENCE IN SECOND REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

I assume, Mr. Speaker, that is recognition. Would the Chair indicate to the house why the Secretary of State last week was told to resume his seat when the Speaker agreed with me, and the remarks are recorded in Hansard, that the Secretary of State had been giving the Chair trouble.
In respect to the recognition of front benchers, the Leader of the Opposition and leaders of other parties, I would once again refer to the fact that nowhere in the rule book do I find that a backbencher is relegated to any inferior position in the house.
We of course recognize the necessity of ministers having the right to rise on these occasions, but not without recognition. The same applies to the leader of my own party, the Leader of the Opposition, and to the leader of any other party. Again I say that nowhere in the rule book do I find a backbencher is relegated to an inferior position. Privileges and Elections notes and lose the thread of his thoughts. That is, Mr. Speaker, what was once said in this house by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne). speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (for the Secretary of State) moved:
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER GREATER DISPATCH OF BUSINESS
speechtext:
That a select committee be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedures and organization of this house, for the purpose of suggesting any changes that would assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business and would strengthen parliament and make it more effective; that the committee have power to send for persons and papers; that it report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house; and that it consist, in addition to Mr. Speaker, of 14 members to be designated at a later date.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the house having decided to suspend for the time being the debate on the matter which has been before it for so many hours, this gives me the opportunity and the honour of moving a motion which stands in the name of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), the importance and urgency of which has been attested to by the leaders of other parties in this house.
This resolution, in itself, and in its substance, is not important unless it were rejected. The importance of it is that it makes possible the establishment of a committee which could be one of the most important committees that has been set up by this house for a long time. It makes possible the establishment of this committee at a time when we are very conscious of the need to change our rules and procedures to make possible the more effective dispatch of the business of this house. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that all hon. members of the house are interested in achieving that objective, subject of course to the preservation of the rights and privileges of individual members and the legitimate traditions of the house.
This committee will examine how to make parliament operate more effectively to deal

with the many, and complicated, and new matters which now customarily come before parliament. The Leader of the Opposition in his intervention yesterday answered certain critics of parliamentary procedure and parliamentary activities, and I agree with him that some of this criticism of the institution of parliament has been unreasonable. Some of it has not taken into account, not only the practices and customs of the past but the real difficulties of the present, in adjusting our parliamentary procedures to the many new and complicated problems that arise.
We hear a great deal of criticism on all sides, both inside and outside the house, of the manners and the methods of parliament; but as the right hon. gentleman did the other day, it is well to recall history on this matter so that we may retain that sense of perspective and proportion which is useful in considering matters of this kind. Even in the mother of parliaments-and I think this was referred to the other day-there have been many examples of filibustering, obstruction and even violent scenes.
One does not have to go too far back, to the days of the Irish nationalists, when the business of the house was held up day after day and when scenes were so wild as to make our scenes, when we have them in the House of Commons, seem pretty mild by comparison. Those of us who have studied and are interested in British parliamentary history are reminded how Mr. Disraeli once felt comforted because there was between himself and the other party the clerk's table, which he referred to as that substantial piece of furniture. We have not needed that in this house, at least in my memory.
Distant pastures and distant parliaments in time and in space always look greener and better. It is similar in this House of Commons, yet anyone with a knowledge of parliamentary history-and the right hon. gentleman referred to this yesterday-and looks back even 50 years ago, will be reminded about the violence of debate at that time, the total obstruction day after day of measures brought in for approval, and of constant challenges. There were the same charges of time wasting which take place even today.
A sense of perspective is good and useful; but that does not mean that we have not very serious problems before the house in the organization and operation of parliamentary business and parliamentary procedures. Furthermore there is a very great difference between now and 50 years ago in the house, a difference which arises out of the nature and the scope of our activities today.
Appointment of Committee
We have infinitely more to do today than they had 50 years ago, and our sessions are now almost continuous throughout the year. It was not so many generations ago when the problem of a prime minister and government of the day was finding enough legislation to keep parliament in session at least two months. There are more decisions to be made now, and these decisions involve more continuous responsibility on parliament, on the opposition and the government, than was the case some years ago.
Therefore the need for efficient procedures and the effective discharge of business with a minimum of delay is much greater now than it was in the days about which I have been talking, and the penalty today for inefficiency is much greater than it used to be in those days. In addition the danger to the public welfare, if we do not order our proceedings effectively, is much greater than it used to be. Perhaps that is the reason that public opinion is much less tolerant than it was 50 years ago of the foibles and weaknesses of parliament, and of the House of Commons in particular.
The consequences of our inaction or wrong action today are very immediate and direct, and far greater on our people because of the greater impact of what we do, due to the necessarily increased intervention of parliament and the government in the life and affairs of average people.
This has been recognized during the last 10 or 15 years, particularly in the House of Commons, and we have made progress in those areas in improving our procedures. We have gone some distance in the last few years in limiting debate, in limiting the time that can be used for the budget debate and for the address in reply to the speech from the throne. We have cut out a good many of the frills, and this has meant an improvement. These changes were made by agreement among all parties, and were mostly made through a committee set up by the house. I might add that in the deliberations of that committee party considerations did not loom as large as they sometimes do in the house. But, Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal more to be done. It seems to me we have just touched the surface in the changes required to make our deliberative assembly more effective.
We have to make some more fundamental changes than have been possible in the past, and it is essential at the same time to maintain the traditions and customs of the house, and the rights of individual members, particularly of individual members in the opposition. I think we can reconcile these two things and I hope this committee will be in a

Provision for Minimum Wage Rate position to make recommendations to that end.
One of the things to which I hope the committee will give active consideration, is how we can make the committees system of the house operate more effectively. This is something we have all talked about in recent years, and the right hon. gentleman had very important plans to that effect from 1957 onwards. I know an effort was made, but I am sure he will agree it was not as successful as he would have hoped. This is no reflection on the attempt that was made; but surely it is now important to treat this problem as one of the most serious problems of parliament-the more effective discharge of work through committees in a way that will give the committees authority and power to make decisions, and when the decisions are referred to the House of Commons we will not have to go through the same debate over and over again that has taken place in the committees.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

the second reading of Bill No. C-28, to provide for minimum wages for employees in federal works, undertakings, and businesses.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to provide for legislation in the federal labour field which is supported by all the parties in this House of Commons. The proposal is that we should have federal legislation providing for a minimum wage. As hon. members are aware, labour matters come partly under provincial jurisdiction and partly under federal jurisdiction, and therefore this bill would provide for a minimum wage only with respect to those employees who come under federal labour jurisdiction. The proposal in my bill is that a minimum wage at the federal level be set at $1.25 an hour. The bill, of course, makes it clear that it would not affect the rate of wages of any employees who already enjoy a higher rate of wages; but if this bill passed and became law it would provide that no one under federal labour jurisdiction could be employed at a rate of less than $1.25 an hour.
Mr. Speaker, minimum wage legislation in the various provinces of Canada is by no means uniform. It varies from province to


province as to the extent of its coverage; it varies from province to province, and from area to area within some provinces, as to the amount that is set as a minimum wage. We feel that the time has come to do two things by legislation of this kind; first of all to provide a minimum wage at the federal level, and second to give a lead to the provinces. It should be stated quite clearly that in the provincial labour field the provinces are autonomous, but it is the view of some of us that if in this area we had good legislation in the federal labour field, it would give a lead to the provinces to make their legislation better than it now is.
The kinds of improvements that are needed in the provinces are such as would extend the coverage to all workers, both male and female, in all areas of our provinces, and also raise the amount of the minimum wage. However, it is not our function here to deal with provincial legislation. I mention those improvements in connection with my suggestion that one of the purposes of federal legislation in this field is to give a lead to the provinces as well.
I said in my opening words that the purpose of this bill is to provide legislation in our federal statute books which is supported by all the parties in this House of Commons. I need not name them all; that list, of course, is growing these days. But I wish to refer in particular to the party that is now in power, the Liberal party. It supports minimum wage legislation, as it supports other legislation in the labour field. In the last parliament, when the Liberals sat in opposition, they readily supported all the labour bills that some of us brought forth. In this parliament they sit on the government side and so they sing a slightly different tune.

I do not deny them that opportunity; I only wish they would avail themselves of the opportunity, now they are on the government side of the house.
On May 30 of this year when we were debating another bill of mine in the labour field, Bill No. C-2, which provided for statutory holidays with pay, when I pointed out to Liberal members that they had supported

this bill in the previous parliament and were now talking it out, the answer was that it was their intention as Liberals to bring in a national labour code, a comprehensive measure that would include all these things. So I was asked to be patient and to wait until later in the session, when a national labour code would be brought in and the Liberals would provide a charter for labour in terms of statutory holidays with pay, adequate annual vacations, minimum wages, maximum hours of work, and all the things that can be part of a national labour code. I was asked to wait, Mr. Speaker. That was on May 30.
Four and a half months have gone by since then. If the Liberals want to think of it in terms of a number of days, that is 135 days, more than twice the number of days the Liberals needed to get things rolling. But not one suggestion has come from the other side of the house that there is in sight a national labour code or any of the elements of such a labour code which the Liberals promised when they were in opposition, when they were on the hustings and even since they came into this house as the government of Canada. Therefore it seems to me that once again we have to call upon the government of the day and its supporters to take the position, now that they are in power, that they took when they were in opposition. If they then believed in things like this, in a national minimum wage of at least $1.25 an hour, I suggest they should show their support for such a proposal when it is brought before them at this time.
We have had an interesting experience with private members' resolutions and bills in this session. At first they were treated according to the pattern of former years; they were all talked out. Then there seemed to be a little revolution amongst some of the backbenchers on the Liberal side. They did not like having to talk out bills that last year they supported, and as a result of that a bit of a reform took place. Some measures, instead of being talked out, were debated for an hour and then their subject matter was sent to whatever was the appropriate committee. While that is not as satisfactory as passing a piece of legislation and sending a bill itself to a committee, it certainly is better than treating an important piece of legislation to the talking out process.
I hope that today hon. members will not again ask us to wait for this national labour code, since we have already waited four and a half months, since the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Gray) and the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne), promised us that these things were coming. I hope that instead they will do either one of two things, support this bill on second reading, whereupon it would be referred to the
Provision for Minimum Wage Rate committee on industrial relations for study as to its detail, or at least give it that better-than-talking-out procedure, that of having its subject matter referred to that same committee, the committee on industrial relations.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that there is no need in this house, made up of the various parties that are here, to argue the merits of a minimum wage bill; that we ought to have this kind of legislation; that we ought to have it at the federal level, and that the rate of wages in any minimum wage bill should be not less than $1.25 an hour. I suggest that since we all agree to this proposition we give this measure that is now before us the best treatment that it can be given in the time at our disposal. If the house, as I think it should, sees fit to agree to second reading, I give the undertaking that I would not then try to move it into committee of the whole, but I would move that.it be referred to the committee on industrial relations for study clause by clause, in all its detail.
If that is not possible, I hope at least that the bill will not be talked out but rather that the subject matter will be sent to that same committee. There, along with other bills which have been referred, it can be studied, so that we can make some progress toward getting the national labour code which the Liberals promised in the election campaign, which they promised on the floor of this house, but any sight of which we have yet to see. Because we all believe in the principle of this bill, I suggest that it should receive the support of the house in this private members' hour.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great deal of pleasure and attention to the comments just made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) concerning Bill C-28, which is meant to provide minimum wages of $1.25 per hour throughout the country.
No doubt that the bill is of some value and deserved to be introduced to prepare public opinion.
It must be borne in mind, however, that our country is quite large and that, from one ocean to the other, interests are many and varied.
The situation in Newfoundland may not be compared with that in Vancouver. The two areas are so different. The climate is different and so are working conditions. That is why it is rather difficult to set certain working conditions to be uniformly applied to all the various parts of the country.
However, I believe that a minimum must necessarily be established. In fact, I think that

Provision for Minimum Wage Rate we must pay particular attention to the condition of the workers in the whole country.
But to say that it must be, everywhere in the country $1.25 an hour, would be to impose a limitation on the salary in some places where it is already above $1.25 an hour and in fact to increase it tremendously in some other places where it is very low, as, for example, where it is only $1 an hour.
It would be difficult, therefore to accept, on a total and permanent basis, the purpose of the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. We know that the object of the bill which he presents to the house is much too serious to be considered lightly. By that I do not mean that the sponsor of the bill did not consider it in detail. He probably did so extensively. The number of sections in the bill shows it. It is easy to see that he worked seriously at it.
But I wonder if all the members have had time to study it carefully, in view of the amount of work they have been called upon to do since the beginning of the session. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has just suggested that it be referred to a committee to be considered in detail.
On the other hand, I know that at the present time the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) is studying a labour code. And, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put it so well, such a study cannot be made hastily; the problems the government has faced since then have been such that we had to put it aside in order to consider more urgent matters.
We recently had before us a resolution and a bill to provide for the placing of the maritime transportation unions of Canada under the management and control of trustees, and every member studied them extensively and every one freely expressed his opinion in the house, so that we are aware of their opinion on that matter.
Since the beginning of the session, we had before us legislative measures requiring the continuous and constant attention of the house. This is the reason why we did not have time to study properly the labour code. But I know that the Minister of Labour is now dealing with a complete consolidation of all acts on labour and their relation with the federal field. This is likely to encourage the provinces to adopt a similar labour code.
For instance, I know that in the province of Quebec only, there is a great difference between wages paid in Hull, in Montreal, in Quebec and in the Gaspe peninsula, because of different conditions prevailing in each of these areas.
The various governments of the province of Quebec, at all times, have often been


blamed for not paying their workmen enough. That is due to the fact that the province should have been divided into areas where salaries could be different and according to the cost of living in each area. I often claimed that when I was a member of the Quebec legislature in 1935-36 and in 1939-45; I always contended that dividing the province into areas would have enabled us to establish salaries according to the circumstances and labour conditions prevailing in each of those areas. But they never paid much attention to me. Today generally salaries are being increased. The federal government did not wait for us to do so, and a complete study is now under way; I do not know how far it will go, but I hope that it will be in the right direction.
The same conditions prevail in the province of Ontario, in the prairie provinces, in the maritimes, and also in the province of British Columbia.
The various parts of Canada are altogether different. The cost of living index is not the same everywhere. We have to consider the index for each part of the country.
I say that it would be a monumental mistake to pass this bill right now and provide for minimum wage of $1.25 throughout Canada, as it would result in a reduction in many localities where salaries are higher and an increase where they are sufficient.
That is why I suggest that this matter should be examined more sensibly and more thoroughly. At any rate, I feel that during the hour we have at our disposal, it would be impossible to examine this bill in a way that would enable us to understand it. I think it would be wise to wait until the Minister of Labour has prepared and submitted to us his labour code. Then, if hon. members are not satisfied with his resolution on the labour code, they could criticize it to their heart's content, and even oppose it, and we shall be in a position to give them the proper answers at that time. We will at least have had the chance to study a comprehensive scheme applicable throughout the country and taking into account different circumstances in any part of the country, an organization which could guide us in some way to attain a certain end. That is why I suggest that the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is ill-timed. It has perhaps been prepared in a hurry. The hon. member may have studied it, but we do not feel that we have had enough time to read it, examine it and understand it fully.
For those reasons, I believe we should vote it down. On the other hand, I know that some hon. members on this side of the house do not share my views, and I realize

also that other members, on the other side of the house do not share them either. I also believe that this matter is bound to be very actively discussed. That is why I do not want to take too much time, because I would like other hon. members to have a chance to express their views.
I therefore say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that I do not wish to accept his bill today, because I think it is premature and that it was too hastily introduced. I think he should give the Minister of Labour a chance to produce his labour code, and then, he may criticize it and perhaps submit certain things provided in this legislation, in the form of amendments. Then, we may all agree and accept it or reject it.
That is what I am asking today, and I hope that those who will rise after me will probably share my views.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not delay hon. members too long, but I would like to make a few remarks in connection with the legislation now before us.
First of all, may I commend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for renewing, in each session, his attempts to move a similar bill. This proves his interest for the working class. It is certainly in a spirit of fairness that he wants to see the workers' salaries under federal jurisdiction, generally increased to $1.25 an hour.
Nowadays, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that a salary of $1.25 is certainly not excessive. I should also tell the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), who preceded me, that I do not quite understand how he can maintain that this bill would, in certain places, bring existing salaries down to $1.25 an hour. I think that the legislation before us covers the case, when it provides that the lowest salary rate should be $1.25. This means, of course, that any salary higher than $1.25, may stay at that higher level.
I cannot agree with the remarks of my hon. friend for Hull (Mr. Caron). In previous years, he has been greatly concerned with improving the workers' lot and he should therefore be congratulated; but I believe that to postpone such a bill from one session to another is only to delude ourselves.
There is also the question of labour unions which should not be forgotten, and this is why, even if I support the allegations of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that it is commendable to increase as much as possible salaries of workers and employees coming under the
Provision for Minimum Wage Rate federal government, I still believe that we should not ignore the influence and authority of labour unions in such a matter.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I believe that it would be profitable to study this bill in the house, as I am convinced that it would be useful to hear the opinions of members before forming an opinion that would really be in the best interest of the workers.
I do not wish to prevent other members from speaking on this bill and this is why I maintain that we should grant it our fullest consideration, because it is of great interest for the working class in our society.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South has sat here for longer than I have and I am always glad to learn, if possible, from a member with longer experience. It is true I have some notes before me, but it has never been my practice in the house to read from a prepared text, nor am I doing so now. The hon. member for Cape Breton South may himself have to resort to a practice of that sort and therefore he presumes I am doing so. That is not the case.
One of the advantages of legislation along the lines suggested would be the placing of additional purchasing power in the hands of those who belong to the lower income groups. This would be a most admirable result. There are, perhaps, those who feel that a minimum wage of $1.25 across Canada might bring about inequities, inasmuch as it is difficult to ascertain whether the effect of $1.25 in one area is the same as in another area. There are some who, for this reason, might prefer to see a lower figure established. They might think, for instance, that $1.10 would be a better figure. I do not agree. We have to arrive at some figure, and I think the figure of $1.25 is a good one. Of course, I have no way of knowing accurately the extra cost which would be involved in making it $1.25 as opposed to $1.10, but from a source which I believe can be regarded as reasonably reliable I learn that if the figure of $1.10 were adopted, some 20,000 to 23,000 people employed in crown corporations and the like would be affected, and that the extra cost involved would be of the order of $6 million. On the other hand, if $1.25 were the figure adopted a far broader group of crown employees would be affected and the extra money involved would be about $17 million. There is a good deal of difference between those two figures. Nevertheless, I think that since legislation of this sort is overdue it would be unwise to set the figure at less than $1.25 an hour. As I said, one of the reasons that a minimum wage of $1.25 an hour would be a benefit to the country is that it would give additional purchasing power to those in the lower income group. There would also be the advantage of equality of income standards throughout Canada.

There is one problem, however, that we have to face and to which the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) has already made some reference. There are areas in Canada where $1.25 an hour certainly means more than it does in other areas. I think this is known to all members and is really an obvious fact. What is really needed, I suppose, is an extensive study, and perhaps the perennial suggestion of $1.25 an hour that has been made in recent years could be approached in this way. There may be some refinements that could be made and possibly in certain areas the figure could be higher than $1.25 an hour. Perhaps some allowances might be made. I would not want to say whether this is a wise or unwise practice. We know that in some provinces there is a difference between the urban rate and the rural rate. I can certainly see the reasoning behind this, but as far as I am concerned the answers are not all in on that question. I am not sure that is a wise course of action.
I thought I had the reference in my notes but when I make notes I unfortunately do not always include all those things I should like to; so in this case I must apologize to the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Maclnnis). I will not be referring to my notes but rather to my memory. If my memory is correct, there are some provinces that do not have a difference between the urban and rural rates, and I think there is something to be said for that. Perhaps a distinction could be made along other lines than the area. Perhaps it could be made on the basis of the type of work in which people are engaged.
I think that these considerations, and the fact that there is much more that could be said on this subject lead us to the conclusion that, while we agree this matter really should have been dealt with a long time ago, we cannot accept the bill without further study. It may be that if the present and previous governments had been as progressive in their legislation as some people would have liked them to be, this problem would have been settled some years ago. As I said at the outset, while I cannot speak for the government I am quite confident that those things that were promised in this regard by Liberal candidates prior to the election will be carried out, and I hope very soon.

The committee has not met since I returned to parliament in 1962 and perhaps this would be something it could consider, particularly if the members of the government party are in fact serious when they say they would like to see some such legislation passed. Certainly it would be useful to them to study the provisions in this bill in order to assist them in drawing up the labour code they have promised.
I believe there are 19 sections in the bill before us. As I look through them I see there is provision for a minimum wage of $1.25 per hour and in addition there are sections providing that there is to be no deduction from the $1.25 per hour for such things as special wearing apparel, special tools, and so on. There is also a provision, I am glad to learn, relating to board and lodging, and so on, if this is supplied by the employer. So, if you add all these things up the minimum wage that would result, that is, the total remuneration actually paid to the employee, would be substantially more than the $1.25 per hour.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think there should be some additional study of this measure. I am not completely familiar with the working conditions in all parts of Canada, nor am I completely familiar with those industries that supply wearing apparel, tools and so on, for which deductions would not be allowed from the $1.25 under the provisions of this

Provision for Minimum Wage Rate bill. Another provision that should have been in this bill, perhaps even in the preamble, is that this $1.25 is a minimum only and should not be considered as a fair wage. There has been a minimum wage law in the province of Alberta for a number of years, but it is made abundantly clear that it is not considered to be a fair wage or a proper wage; it is simply a minimum. I think this should be made clear also in any federal statute which attempts to set a minimum, that it should not be considered as a fair wage.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I would support the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in his plea to have the bill sent to the committee on industrial relations, or some other committee for study.
