speakeroldname: Hon. J. P. Deschatelets (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, since the items submitted to the hon. members were prepared under the previous administration, over a year ago, I don't think it is necessary for me to give you a long explanation.
However, we have slightly changed those estimates and to enable the house to get a better understanding of the various projects and amounts you are called upon to approve,
I intend to give you some essential explanations and I will do it alternatively in French and in English.

As you know, Mr. Chairman, the items under the heading of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation must be excluded as they now fall under the jurisdiction of the Minister of National Revenue. As for the items concerning the national capital commission, I shall deal with them separately after the items of the Department of Public Works are completed. You will recall that when these items were tabled by the Minister of Finance in May 1963 he also announced that we would be reviewing these estimates to ensure that the amounts were realistic and that they would reflect as accurately as possible what the department could actually carry out this fiscal year.

When revising the estimates prepared in September and October 1962, we found that some projects could not be undertaken because of local difficulties such as the selection of the site, or because of changes in the plans or because of new needs that occurred since 1962. Some projects represent a reduction in the original amount but on the other hand this reconsideration of projects indicated that in some other cases an additional amount had to be provided for to ensure completion of the work.

The net effect of this is that of the total amount indicated in the main estimates for public works for 1963-64, to wit $166 million, a sum of $7,391,195 will not be required and appropriate amendments will be introduced when the individual items are called. On the other hand, additional amounts were required for new programs or projects which could be undertaken within the fiscal year. These additional items will be found listed in the supplementary estimates of the public works department and amount to $12.8 million.

In a word, I would now ask you to approve a total of $172.3 million, and there is an

amount of $6.3 million provided for by the previous administration. For the items we are preparing for the year 1964-65 I expect a more important increase. I will then take that opportunity to submit to the hon. member my idea of the part that the Department of Public Works must play in the national economy. At that time I will have visited the major part of the main projects under construction in the country and I hope that the next estimates that are submitted to the house will reflect the progressive emphasis I intend to give that department which can do so much to develop strategic areas in our various provinces.

I know hon. members will appreciate these facts and that I can count on their fullest co-operation in considering these estimates. I will endeavour to provide answers to any questions they may have. However, I would propose that I deal with them after all members concerned have completed their observations.

Before I resume my seat, may I express to the entire staff of the department my admiration and my appreciation for the dedication they have shown since last April and I wish to tell them how gratifying it is to work with servants of the country who have such a fine comprehension of the importance of their responsibilities.
When I leave that office, maybe in some 20 years, I hope that the department will enjoy as much prestige as it did when I took over.

Mr. Chairman, my first remarks will be to offer my best wishes to the new incumbent of the public works portfolio. And I could not offer him better wishes than to follow in the steps of his predecessor. I think it will be the best way for him to build up for himself an enviable reputation, to be a man of whom it can be said that he has rendered services to his country.
The Hon. Davie Fulton who left the federal field to go into the provincial political arena was an excellent minister and I know that all members of the house agree to that and miss him a lot. We, on this side of the house, wish him the best of luck in his new political career.
Mr. Chairman, the minister gave us a concise statement of the various changes made within the Department of Public Works and indicated his intention to recommend some others in the future.
Besides, we deeply regretted that when the new administration took office the Department
Supply-Public Works of Public Works was handicapped in matters concerning the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. We think it would have been more logical to have the business of that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation administered by the public works department rather than by the national revenue department.
Did the government try to curtail the importance of that department since the incumbent was from Quebec or did the government consider the minister incapable of managing the business of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation?
Small politics.

In the course of my remarks, I do not intend to go into details.
I only want to make a broad review, but I would like later to ask a few questions concerning certain secondary items.
There have been many changes since the minister was named to the Department of Public Works. His first act was to have an office installed in Montreal, at the expense of the Department of Public Works. We would like to know, on this side of the house, what was the cost of this installation, since it is a precedent, and we would also like to know the reasons why the minister, who is almost continually busy in Ottawa, had this office installed.
We would be happy to know who acts for him while he is absent from Montreal. Who are the persons assigned to that office? I was told there are four persons. We would like to know about their salaries, their wages and the part they play, for we find it strange, on this side of the house, that the minister should have in Montreal such a large staff and an office in the public works department building. We would not wish it to be a den for patronage. We wish the minister would give us explanations on that question.
May I remind the minister that one of his first acts as Minister of Public Works was to attend in Montreal, on June 3, 1963, the opening of tenders for work to be carried out at the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary.
We should also like to have some information in that connection. Would the minister tell us whether he will continue to open tenders himself and whether it is the usual practice for a minister of the crown to do that?
According to the Montreal newspapers, after the opening of the tenders, the minister communicated directly with Argo Construction to give them the news and to ask them if they were interested in getting the contract. Mr. Chairman, we find such a behaviour very odd on the part of a minister of the crown.

Supply-Public Works
As I said a while ago, the minister opened an office in Montreal. I have no hesitation to say publicly here that the officials ol the Department of Public Works in Montreal cannot act freely, according to their conscience and their oath of allegiance. The representatives of the minister in Montreal do not allow any employee there to take his responsibilities and to do his duty. They interfere constantly, keep watch over the departmental officials and thwart their efforts. The employees work under tension all the time and we should like the minister to give us some explanation in that respect.
Mr. Chairman, I feel it is unusual for people from the minister's office, in other words proteges of the minister, to try to impede officials of the Department of Public Works in the accomplishment of their duties.
It is true that at the beginning of his remarks, the minister paid a tribute to the employees of this department stating that he was ready to co-operate with them. But if the minister wishes really to be logical with himself, he will begin by closing his Montreal office, he will ask his representatives to refrain from putting pressure on the employees of the Department of Public Works and let them take their decisions and carry out their work.
We, on this side of the house, wish to do without either good or bad patronage, as was the practice up to 1957. I warn the minister that we will be on the watch and I will take this opportunity to remind the house of the kind of patronage which always existed under the Liberal regime before 1957.
Mr. Chairman, I have in hand a photostat letter written by an official of the Department of Publics Works in Montreal which I wish to put on the official record. It reads as follows:

In the first letter, written under a government to which the minister belonged, and I know that he will certainly not fail his friends-

Mr. Chairman, you have a letter from the former government of which the hon. member for Hull and the present Minister of Public Works were members. On the other hand, when we were in office, we sent a letter to superintendents of buildings, letting them know that they were completely free to act as they saw fit, according to their conscience and in keeping with the oath they had taken.
There is the difference. That is why I am informing the Minister of Public Works that we shall keep our eyes open and maintain a constant watch.
Newspapers having reported that the minister had had an office built in Montreal, in which four representatives persecute, so to speak, and watch continuously the officials of the Department of Public Works in Montreal, who cannot make an inspection or give instructions without everything being censured by those favorites of the Minister of Public Works, we cannot but ask that this system be abolished.

Mr. Chairman, we want to co-operate with the minister, but we ask him to act according to democratic principles. Our forefathers, English as well as French speaking, fought to keep a close watch on the money spent by the state. Mr. Chairman, the minister's statement was very short.

Mr. Chairman, I shall answer the question, but I think that suggestion made by the hon. member for Cochrane is completely out of order, since it concerns what is said to have happened in the province of Quebec. If the hon. member wants to deal with provincial politics, let him resign.
Mr. Chairman, as long as I comply with the rules of the house, the hon. member cannot prevent me from saying what I think, according to my conscience, because as far as we who sit on this side of the house are concerned our conscience is clear.
Mr. Chairman, the type of letter sent by the Department of Public Works in 1954 is a scandal which we do not want to be repeated. And I insist on telling to the minister that we shall do our duty, that we shall scrutinize and watch his actions. I know that the minister is a fine man, but we do not want him to be too much influenced by the hon. member for Laurier.
We, on this side of the house, are willing to co-operate fully with the minister so long as he will provide us with the information we request. I feel that the people must be fully informed about the estimates and that the opposition must scrutinize them.
We want to get the list of suppliers of furniture to the department since the minister was appointed to that office.
We also want to know whether tenders have been called and whether they were public tenders, and, in every case, the names of the tenderers and the amounts involved.
We want to know too if tenders have been called for heating fuel intended for public buildings throughout Canada.
We want to know the names of the tenderers, if possible, by provinces. I believe, Mr. Chairman, that we have a right to get such information.
When the Minister of Public Works was in the opposition, I remember that he rose in the house with such a sad face that you would have thought he had been crying, and in a sobbing voice he said that unemployment was such a dreadful thing. It is true. If the present government had let us proceed with our work, we would have found a solution

much more easily than the Liberal administration is doing at the present time.
Do you know, Mr. Chairman, what the minister has done. This minister who was crying reminded me of those Buddhist monks who burn themselves up, as you probably know. He was weeping over the unemployed. But do you know what he has done? The first thing he did was to open an office in Montreal.
The second one was to cancel many projects included in the estimates which we had drawn up.
At the present time, unemployment is crucial in Canada. Forty per cent of the unemployed are in the province of Quebec. There are also unemployed people in all the other provinces of the country.
Do you know, Mr. Chairman, that it is as a result of an answer given to a question put on the order paper that I learned about the cancellation of works for a value of $2.45 million for this year by the Minister of Public Works. Why, Mr. Chairman, at a time where the government knows that it is faced with a crucial unemployment problem, a serious problem threatening the economic foundations of the country, why has the minister cancelled $2.45 million of works in the country?
I have the list in hand. For example, in Nova Scotia, almost $400,000 of public works were cancelled. In the province of Quebec, almost $315,000 of works and as much in Ontario. I could give you a detailed list. I would like the minister to explain why these works have been cancelled, while they appeared in the main estimates.
We would also like to know, if these works have been considered as being reasonable by qualified officials of the Department of Public Works why the minister has left them out and whether the minister intends in the near future to carry out these building projects, in order that we may know whether the minister or the officials of the department are inconsequential. But I have more confidence, Mr. Chairman, in the distinguished officials of the Department of Public Works who are logical and qualified employees-the architects, engineers and others who have proved themselves.
I naturally have all due respect for lawyers, Mr. Chairman but to my mind the minister was not qualified to determine whether or not $2 million worth of public works could be cancelled in a country afflicted with crucial unemployment.
I am coming back to that. The minister's eyes were full of tears, Mr. Chairman. But today the minister cancels important works in our provinces, at the very moment when unemployment has reached a crucial peak.

I would like now, Mr. Chairman, to give the house a concrete instance which refers to the county I have the honour of representing here. I am thinking about the tenders which were called for the purchase, in the municipality of Rawdon, of a lot to build a post office. The old one was housed in the municipal building.
The mayor and the municipal authorities got in touch with me to inform me that they needed space and they asked for the construction of a post office. Everything was according to the requirements set up by the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works, as far as revenue was concerned.
Then, at the request of the municipal authorities, I made some inquiries. The post office was not for your humble servant. The land was bought, the tenders were called and the lowest bidder was a person from Rawdon.
At that point there was a change of government. The present Minister of Public Works was appointed. He got patronage rolling and this was related to the first move, very likely to favour one of his friends in Montreal. He sent a notice to the contractor who had been awarded the contract and had already started construction, telling him to send his bill, so he could be paid.
The work was stopped, while it was known that the contractor was qualified and that he had been duly approved by the Department of Public Works. I had to beg the minister so that construction could go on. Several days later, he ordered the contractor to carry on with the work of that post office.
I know, Mr. Chairman that this case, which affected me and struck me, has certainly been a shock also to other members of this house.
We should like the Department of Public Works or rather the Minister of Public Works, because I do not want to say anything against the department since the employees of that department do a good job as long as there is no interference from the minister.
We would like all the ridings in the country to be treated the same way, whatever their political allegiance. If the minister wants to do that, he has only to follow the example set by his predecessor, the Hon. Davie Fulton, who was deeply missed by all members of the house and the employees of his department when he left.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the minister must not forget the election promises made by his leader and his party during the last election campaign. In every city or town he visited, the Prime Minister promised something, either the construction of a public building or a wharf. You know, he reminded me a
Supply-Public Works little of the Larousse dictionary: "He sowed broadcast". He made promises.
I read in La Presse on February 27, 1963:
Mr. Pearson promises again a deep water harbour to Riviere du Loup.
The political party which, once in power, will give Riviere du Loup suitable harbour facilities-
Mr. Pearson made promises and I know that he did so in all the provinces of Canada and in the maritimes; now, the minister comes before the house and asks for $172.3 million. He adds only $6.3 million.
I am convinced that those $6.3 million will not take care of all the election promises made by the leader himself. In view of the fact that the minister asks for $6.3 million in supplementary estimates, why did he cut $2,045,000? There is something illogical in this.
We would like also to know what the minister thinks of the famous tax on building materials. I admit that this tax does not fall directly under the Department of Public Works, but I believe that it has direct consequences since it contributes to increase the cost of building materials and, accordingly, has an effect on the construction of buildings by private enterprise in our country. Let me also call to the attention of the minister that the architects and the engineers of the Department of Public Works very often give evidence of bad taste in their building plans. Changes should be made along that line. In other words, attention should be drawn to designing a style proper to each place. If a post office is built in the Laurentians, it should have a special design which would be different from a city post office.
I also ask the Minister of Public Works to set up air conditioning systems in all large public buildings where there are none at the present time. I would give as an example the building where the unemployment insurance and post office employees in Joliette work. It is a beautiful building but it is not equipped with air conditioning; during the summer, for security reasons, they are prohibited from opening the windows to eliminate the risks of thefts. I must admit that no theft has as yet been committed since the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) has been in office.

To continue with my remarks, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that the present government jeopardized the world exhibition every time it delayed that project.
In postponing the choice of a final site for the exhibition the present government wanted to blackmail the authorities of the city of Montreal. One of the commissioners, who is a good friend of the minister, and whose name I will not divulge, told me and others that the government was responsible for the delays and that it had endangered the future of the world exhibition to be held in Montreal. The minister did not want the exhibition to be held on St. Helen's and Notre Dame islands. He is quite aware of the article I have in mind and, since then, he has promised that the world exhibition would be held in the eastern part of the metropolis.
Could we know whom you are speaking of?
I have the article here.
You said that you would not mention the name of a certain party.
I said that the world exhibition commissioner had told me the delays concerning the final acceptance-
Then, it is anonymous?

-had jeopardized the 1967 world exhibition. Besides, Mr. Chairman, I have here La Presse of March 20, 1963.
May I be allowed to point out that during the last election, the minister, who would have been trustee of the world exhibition, as we might say, in the case of a trusteeship, as is evidenced in a letter published in the Montreal newspapers, and mentioned by La Presse and I quote:
The 1967 World Exhibition in Montreal East.
Enclosed you will find copy of a letter which I have addressed to the Chief Commissioner of the 1967 world exhibition, Mr. Paul Bienvenu, as regards the site of the world exhibition.
I did that at the request of various businessmen's associations of the east end of Montreal.-Jean Paul Deschatelets, member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont.
Dear Mr. Bienvenu,
I am writing to you as a citizen of the Montreal east end about the decision that will be reached these next few days as to the site of the 1967 world exhibition.
Many representations have been made concerning the advantages offered by the eastern part of Montreal, the main ones being as follows:
First, a site ready to be developed.
Second, a very cheap site.
Third, a very easily accessible site.
Fourth, a site located in the heart of French Canada.

I hope the east end of Montreal will be recognized as the logical site for the world exhibition and rest assured that this will meet with the opinion of all the experts who have studied the advantages of the various locations which have been submitted to you until now.-Jean Paul Deschatelets, M.P.
Also, Mr. Chairman, there was a question asked on the orders of the day of December 12, 1962, concerning the world exhibition and its site in the Montreal east end, as shown in Hansard at page 2578, and I quote:
1.	Has the associate minister of national defence received briefs from the Montreal east businessmen's association and the municipal council of Ville de Repentigny suggesting Maisonneuve park nr some other location in Montreal east, as the site of the 1967 world fair to be held in Montreal?
2.	Has the attention of the minister been drawn to the fact that there is in Montreal east an 800-acre piece of land available as a site for the world fair?
3.	Before a decision is taken in this connection, will public bodies, such as the businessmen's association and the municipal council of Ville de Repentigny, be consulted?
That was meant to show you, Mr. Chairman, that we are not too surprised that the government took some time before accepting St. Helen's island and Notre Dame island as the site of the world exhibition, which location was the choice of the authorities of the city of Montreal.
I should also like to underline, Mr. Chairman, the excellent work done by Mr. Paul Bienvenu who, faced with situation which he described as untenable, could not carry on. I offer my best wishes to the new commissioner, Mr. Pierre Dupuy.
May I congratulate publicly here, in this house, the mayor of Montreal for the excellent work he has performed and for his contribution to the success of the exhibition. I am convinced that the mayor of Montreal keeps working towards the success of this exhibition.
Mr. Chairman, may I also pay a tribute to a man who was the first person in Canada to advocate that the world exhibition be held in Montreal in 1967, and I am referring to the late Senator Mark Drouin. He has gained our gratitude and everybody knows this outstanding personality asserted himself for the manner in which he interpreted Canada. I say: Hats off for the work he performed in connection with the Montreal world exhibition of 1967.
Mr. Chairman, after an inexcusable delay, Ottawa, by dint of pressure from all sides, and of complaints on the part of the Canadian public, gives its assent to the St. Helen's island site.
The federal government also forced the authorities of the city of Montreal to pay the
Supply-Public Works sum of $2,500,000 for part of an ice control project.
Mr. Chairman, I have here an article published in the Montreal paper La Presse on Thursday, July 4, 1963, entitled:
Montreal attributes all difficulties concerning the world exhibition to Ottawa.
The city of Montreal availed itself yesterday of the new delay brought about by next Saturday's "summit conference'', to stiffen its attitude toward the federal authorities and, finally, to blame "the people in Ottawa" as being solely responsible for the delays in determining the 1967 world exhibition site.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that those are things of the past, that they belong to history today, but I merely wanted to recall in the beginning, that the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont, who is now the Minister of Public Works and responsible for the world fair, had some rather painful experiences.
Indeed, this government has known the same difficulties, for any legislation introduced in the house was only passed with great effort. Mr. Chairman, it is not surprising that the Minister of Public Works had to face those difficulties, considering the position of his government.
Mr. Chairman, I am saying all this as spokesman for the official opposition in matters pertaining to the Department of Labour estimates, and I can hear a minister of the crown, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Teillet), who is forever passing remarks. I shall therefore ask you, once for all, to invite him to leave the house if he persists in interrupting me. On the other hand, if he wants to ask me any question, let him rise to do so and I shall be pleased to answer him.
Mr. Chairman, I intended to ask some questions, but it would have been very difficult. Anyway, I was tired of just hearing him read from newspaper cuttings.

Mr. Chairman, it might well be said that this government has not been able to rule in peacetime. The president of the world exhibition, as well as one of the commissioners, have resigned. And so has Mr. Claude Robillard. We shall be happy to hear from the minister who is going to replace them. Days and weeks are passing and nobody has been replaced yet. I think this could very well jeopardize the world exhibition planning.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:

whether the hon. member knows that, hardly two weeks ago, the mayor of Montreal stated that the Hon. Mr. Dupuy would probably be the only competent man to fill this post.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. Mr. Dupuy is the only competent person, I would

Supply-Public Works ask the government to give him immediately the status of commissioner general of the world exhibition, so that he could get out of the civil service. I think that as an ambassador he was under the federal cabinet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister

Mr. Chairman, if Mr. Dupuy comes under the jurisdiction of the federal cabinet, I believe that the situation is abnormal because we must give the commissioner general every possible latitude. And we would not want him to be under any influence of the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, I know that Mr. Dupuy enjoys great prestige and that he is a very valuable man. I am also assured that in co-operation with the proper authorities he will ensure the proper operation of the world exhibition. However, we would not want him to be put in an untenable situation.
For these reasons, and following the questions of the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) we would like to know when the government will grant him official status as commissioner general for the exhibition in order that he may cease to be subservient to the federal cabinet.
Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister of Canada knew on July 8 last that Mr. Bienvenu was to resign. Why was there a delay? Why have they waited so long before appointing a successor? I believe that this delay harmed the world fair project.
Mr. Chairman, as I said already, Mr. Dupuy is a competent man and if the government wants to rely on him entirely he will be able to make a success of the exhibition.
Many organizations such as the Jaycees in the district of Montreal expressed a desire that the mayor of Montreal be appointed as commissioner general.
For one, as soon as Mr. Bienvenu resigned, I knew that many citizens of Montreal and the surrounding area declared that in their opinion the mayor of Montreal was highly competent to be at the helm of the exhibition project. Now, when does the government intend to amend the act.

Mr. Chairman, 1 hear another remark by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. Does he have something to say?
Mr. Chairman, a while ago, through sheer courtesy, the house allowed the hon. member to extend his time. But what is he doing? He is only reading newspapers. That is what I had to say.

Mr. Chairman, I have here some paper clippings and some texts I wrote myself. Besides, the spokesman of the official

opposition was always allowed to make his remarks as he pleased, provided he was not out of order.
Just the same, it must make sense.
I warn the minister-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. I have no desire to be discourteous to the hon. member who has the floor, but it does seem to me it would be fair to point out that there are other members of the committee who would like to participate in the discussion this evening. In view of the fact that we are in committee I wonder, on the point of order, whether the hon. member would be willing to bring to a conclusion the particular phase of the remarks with which he is now dealing and perhaps participate later in the debate with some of the other matters with which he might wish to deal.

I agree, Mr. Chairman. I will speak for only a few minutes and I will continue later with the other items. I will do that with pleasure.

Mr. Chairman, as far as the world fair is concerned, I shall have an opportunity to come back to that and the minister might indicate when we can discuss that matter, since there is absolutely nothing in the estimates.
We want the fair to be a success. We want it to get a complete autonomy and we want to see the fair commissioners absolutely free. In other words, we do not want the chosen theme "Man and his World" to become "Liberals and their World" because of patronage.
I wish to warn the trustee minister, under trusteeship, because lately, a committee of the Canada Council was set up for the exhibition and I understand that following certain pressures, the presidency was entrusted to the treasurer of the Liberal party, Senator Gelinas.
And with this, Mr. Chairman, I bring my remarks to a close.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to express my thanks to some hon. members who have yielded the floor to me because of some personal reasons which oblige me to leave early tonight. I wish to extend my gratitude to these hon. members.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) introduces tonight the estimates of his department and among those estimates, the one I consider the most

important of course, the item concerning the Montreal world fair.
As a member from the Montreal area, I must point out certain developments which took place after the election, by accident, of a Liberal government on April 8 last.
As soon as he took over, the Minister of Public Works immediately compromised the potential success, the possible success of the world fair. Mr. Chairman, I wish to call to the attention of the house the fact that the 1967 world fair, which is to be held in Montreal, is one of the most splendid undertakings carried out by the Conservatives during their administration in Ottawa. We owe this to the drive of a government which foresaw that Canada would regain its international position if it could persuade the Paris international bureau of exhibitions that the 1967 world fair should take place in Montreal.
Without minimizing the credit which is due to the mayor of Montreal and to the chairman of the executive council, Mr. Lucien Saulnier, I deem it necessary to point out that from the very beginning the Conservatives were the ones who advocated the idea of a world fair first in Canada, and later on in Montreal.
Close on the heels of the last general election, a palpable uneasiness made itself felt within the World Exhibition Corporation, which should be free from political pressure and from the interference of the new government. Unfortunately, it has not been so. I would not want to see my hon. friends opposite claim that the few remarks I am making tonight concerning political pressures are false.
In order to try to place the problem in a context quite favourable to our friends of the government, I should like simply to quote a few words from an article published in MacLean's magazine of October 5, 1963, at page 17. This magazine's reporter stated in a feature article on the world fair:

The first commissioner general of the fair and his deputy have resigned because of bickering and power-plays by government.

If that is not, Mr. Chairman, a formal charge about undue political pressure exerted by the new Liberal government, within that company, then I ask the minister to refute publicly this assertion, and in particular to prove that there has been no pressure because I am able to establish that there has been some pressure exerted by some Liberal organizers who have become today senior officials and executive assistants to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne).
Supply-Public Works
Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that besides the political pressure which is exerted, we have the misrepresentations and the evasive answers from the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister himself.
I shall say later that the Prime Minister lied deliberately to the house when he gave an answer based on false information from-

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege.

Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege, the hon. member for St. Mary just said that both the Prime Minister and myself had lied or had given some facts which were not accurate, and that we knew they were not accurate. I do not think that this should go on the record unchallenged. I should think that the hon. member for St. Mary should be asked to withdraw these unfortunate and untrue assertions.

Mr. Chairman, I said clearly- and I think the Minister of Public Works heard me quite well-that the Prime Minister had lied to the house or had misinformed the house, because he did not know the facts. I prefer to think that the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister did not lie to the house but rather misinformed its members, probably because they were not aware of the facts that were made public later on.
To prove what I have just said, I would like to recall to the Minister of Public Works the letter of resignation- iText]

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am sure the hon. member for St. Mary would not want anything on the record which would be offensive to him or to any member of this house. Perhaps he might be willing to withdraw what he said, or rephrase it.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I specified that either the Prime Minister lied or that he gave an answer which was not in accordance with the facts, and I prefer to think that it was the latter. But I did not accuse either one of them.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think the hon. member should withdraw the word "lied". It is a most unparliamentary word.

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentlemen in power think that I am hurting their feelings when I say that the Prime Minister has lied, then I did not make that statement; it is for them to believe that. I just put the dilemma to the government-

speechtext:
Order. The hon. member will realize that it is not a question

Supply-Public Works of the feelings of any member of the committee. It is a question of using language which is not permitted in the chamber.

Mr. Chairman, I yield to your demands because I want to be more courteous to the present government than they have been since the session started. I want to say that the Prime Minister may not have lied, but the facts reveal that we did not get the true information when we asked questions of the government on the very issue of the resignation of both the commissioner general and the deputy commissioner. I want to point out to hon. gentlemen that when Mr. Bien-venu resigned his function it was acknowledged that things were not going so well. On July 19 I asked the Prime Minister if either Mr. Carsley or Mr. Bienvenu were asked to resign, or whether they had informed the government of their intention to resign. On that occasion both the Minister of Public Works and the Prime Minister answered that all was well under the roof of the World Fair Corporation, that no such thing was true and that this statement did not conform with the truth. When Mr. Bienvenu made public his letters of resignation, it was found that the first letter sent to the Prime Minister was dated July 12, 1963, which was six days before the Prime Minister answered in this house that he was not aware that either Mr. Bienvenu or Mr. Carsley were resigning.
That is on the record, and I am sure the Minister of Public Works cannot deny something which has been printed in the papers and to which he can refer. It is to this I was referring when I said the Prime Minister did not give an answer to the question I asked on July 13, 1963.

Mr. Chairman, I intend to continue showing that it is unfortunate that the government, as soon as it took office, started to interfere in the business of the World Fair Corporation, using it as a field for political patronage.
By the time the debate on the estimates of the Minister of Public Works is over, I shall be able to give other details.
But to illustrate that there are indications of political pressures, I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to a letter sent by the mayor of Montreal, Mr. Jean Drapeau, on July 2, 1963, to the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Prime Minister of Canada.
I do not intend to read this letter in full, because it is rather long, but I want to point out to the house that certain indiscretions have been committed by the Prime Minister
[The Deputy Chairman.]
and the Minister of Public Works, which were a threat to the success of the world fair.
Those indiscretions were made in regard to the chief organizer of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, during the last federal election.
1 refer to the letter dated July 2, 1963, from which I quote a few paragraphs:
Back in Montreal, we met nobody and we had no telephone conversations with newspaper reporters or anybody else about our meeting and the subject of our conversations.
Besides we were very surprised, Mr. Saulnier and myself, to learn when we arrived at your residence-
Here he meant the residence of the Prime Minister-
-that a telephone call was awaiting Mr. Saulnier.
Later on we found that it was a call from Mr. Brady who had been informed of our visit by someone from your office or the office of Mr. Des-chatelets. At any rate, Mr. Saulnier did not call Mr. Brady back and we returned to Montreal without getting in touch with anyone in Ottawa.
Well then, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the Minister of Public Works to tell us who Mr. Brady is. What was a political organizer like Mr. Brady doing at a confidential meeting between the Prime Minister, the mayor of Montreal and the chairman of the executive council?
That is what leads me to believe that by exerting uncalled for pressure, the Liberal party tried to turn the world fair into a political plum, into a source of patronage, instead of carrying it out as a national endeavour designed to stimulate the interest of foreign countries in Canada.
Later on, that is September 4, 1963, I sent a telegram to the Prime Minister.
In view of the facts I have just mentioned, I felt there was sufficient reason for the house to go into committee or for setting up a special commission of inquiry to determine the true motives behind the resignations of Mr. Bienvenu, the commissioner general, and of Mr. Carsley, his deputy.
If the minister, indeed, if the government has nothing to hide I would hope that a parliamentary committee would be set up to find out the truth, even if the committee had to sit behind closed doors.
Mr. Chairman, I should not want to limit myself only to the uncertainty which was created by the hesitation, the beating about the bush, the delays, the retreat, in short, the carelessness shown by the Minister of Public Works with respect to the world fair since the election of the government, last April 8.
I wish to put on official record the fact that the Liberals have accused the former government of wavering. Now, allow me to

mention that within a month, the Conservative party had chosen the present site of the world fair and had officially accepted it, while the present government took five months to accept definitely and officially the site of St. Helen's island which had been recommended by the former government.
Well, Mr. Chairman, not only should we consider those matters, but also if we are aware of our responsibilities, we should make suggestions to the Minister of Public Works, in order to ensure the success of this world fair.
I would like the minister to consider immediately the possibility of building, in co-operation with the city of Montreal, some access roads to Notre Dame island. I would also like the minister to visit the premises and realize that it would be necessary to widen, in co-operation with the authorities of the province of Quebec, the roadway of Jacques Cartier bridge, and this in the near future.
I would like the Minister of Public Works to consider immediately the building of a throughway around the city of Montreal in order to speed up the flow of traffic to the site of the world fair in Montreal.
I also feel that Canada should decide in the near future what type of pavilion it intends to build and that after the exhibition, this pavilion should be used as a museum of Canadian history, as a hospital or as a cancer research centre.
After all the promises the Prime Minister made during the last two election campaigns, the Minister of Public Works should convince him to give the country a Canadian flag which could wave over this Canadian pavilion at the world fair.
In my opinion, the Minister of Public Works should offer favourable conditions to private enterprise for the building of hotels or facilities to accommodate the many tourists who, I hope, will come to Canada for this event.
There were many other matters I wanted to discuss and I would have liked the Minister of Public Works to explain in his statement how he intends to ease unemployment in the province of Quebec where unemployment affects about 40 per cent of the labour force.
When the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont was in the opposition, I remember that he has accused the Union Nationale government of being responsible for the unemployment situation, because, as he then suggested, the Union Nationale had refused to participate in joint programs. Well, let the hon. minister continue saying the same thing now.

Marked drop of unemployment, more particularly in the province of Quebec.

40 per cent of Canadians unemployed are living in the province of Quebec.

Does the hon. member work hand in hand with the premier of the province of Quebec, who was elected because he promised to put an end to unemployment? I represent a riding where the majority of voters are working people. 1 meet those people and they tell me about their idleness. speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member will recognize that he has wandered quite a bit from the first item now before us by making a review of the political situation in his province.

Mr. Chairman, I must admit that the comments of our hon. friends opposite did sidetrack me a little.
Mr. Chairman, I was asking the Minister of Public Works what steps he intends to take to reduce unemployment.
I know that some parties made suggestions, but I also know-and that is the important

point-that the Liberal party made some too. And that is the purpose of my contribution, to ask the Minister of Public Works to describe to us the program he intends to apply in order that this winter we do not have to suffer from that plague of unemployment, which will increase if the government does nothing. We are interested in that problem, as we used to be when we were in office. And if some members doubt that my statements are correct, I shall quote figures to prove them.
Mr. Chairman, I say to the Minister of Public Works that it is his duty to take immediate steps to reassure the population of the province of Quebec, especially the unemployed, whose number reaches 40 per cent of the total for Canada, and who hope that the Liberal government will take steps to stem unemployment and secure full employment.
Mr. Chairman, I have many more remarks to make, but I shall conclude with some suggestions for the minister. I do not know if it is necessary, but it seems to me that without suggestions, the Liberal government does not work as it should. Here are some of the suggestions I want to make to the minister.
To begin with, the minister will have to intensify right away urban renewal in Montreal. The slums must be demolished and replaced by salubrious houses. Too many people live in slums, in houses that are falling to pieces, and I think that the Minister of Public Works should consult with his colleagues from the cabinet in order that immediate measures may be taken to improve that situation. In doing so, he would help alleviate unemployment.
I say again to him that he will have to promote urban renewal in the city of Montreal.
The minister should also undertake immediately the construction of access roads to the site of the world fair.
Moreover, the Minister of Public Works should tell us whether he intends to recommend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) the removal of that odious 4 per cent tax on building materials, which will be increased to 11 per cent this winter, so that the contractors and taxpayers who would like to do so may build houses this winter, thus increasing employment during that bad season.
Mr. Chairman, I am waiting for the minister's answers. I have many other suggestions to make but I will keep them for later.
Mr. Chairman, of the 21 ridings in the city of Montreal, that of St. Mary is the only one represented by a Conservative member. During the last election campaign, the electors

of the city of Montreal were the victims of propaganda published by some partisan newspapers. Personally, I was logical with my electors, and they in turn were quite logical with me, so that we might not be all victims of that propaganda. I am amazed to note that out of the 21 members from Montreal, there is only one to rise in the house and ask, for the city of Montreal, the metropolis of Canada, the carrying out of important works. The present government should do something for the metropolis of Canada just as we did when we were in power.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not detain the committee very long because there are others who would like to speak this evening and I have not as much to say as the speakers who preceded me. As you know, Mr. Chairman, I will be leaving in a day or two and I will not return to the house for three weeks, so there will be silence from this quarter. I should like to move from the past into the future for a moment.
I have a peculiar problem which I should like to present to the minister, and it is related to the paving of the Alaska highway. I realize, of course, that this highway comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence at the moment. However, I should like to ask the minister to do some more transferring and get the Alaska highway transferred to his department. I quite understand that as long as the Department of National Defence has jurisdiction, the paving of the highway is something in which they would not be interested. I can assure the minister, however, that the paving of that highway is something in which not only the people of that particular part of the country are interested but many other people as well, including the minister of northern affairs. He is especially interested, and has been most energetic in trying to get something done along that line.
I would appreciate it very much if some negotiations could be conducted with a view to having the Alaska highway paved and reconstructed. I understand that British Columbia is prepared to pay one third of the cost of this project in the British Columbia section, which certainly would be a great help to the federal Department of Public Works, if that department should assume jurisdiction over this highway.
Then, I should like to interest the Minister of Public Works in considering proposals which have been put forward on a number of occasions during election campaigns by both the Liberal and Conservative parties, that is a trans-Canada highway system. In my 28902-5-2401
Supply-Public Works view this is an important step. I like to qualify this request by saying that if the federal government ceases to take the lion's share of the tax revenues and thus allow the provincial governments to embark upon a greater highway program, then I would drop my request immediately. Under the circumstances, since I am convinced the federal government is taking the lion's share of the tax revenue, I believe some responsibility does devolve upon the department.
There is one other thing I should like to mention, and again the minister of northern affairs is involved. I have a feeling that most people who use the trans-Canada highway or other trunk highways over which the federal government might have jurisdiction could be given a right of way when they pass through national parks. I believe that the amount of money that is involved in collecting this $2 from individuals who pass through these parks would provide a right of way through the park. Then, people who are not interested in stopping in the national parks and who are using a through, trans-continental highway, could travel unimpeded through these parks. I have been told by trucking firms that it is very much easier to enter the United States at Coutts or Sweet Grass and come out at Sault Ste. Marie, than it is to go through one of the national parks. I do not think this should be the case. I feel the time has come when serious consideration should be given to eliminating what I believe is an absolute nuisance for travellers on our highways.
I have just one or two little reminders left which, as the hon. member for Kootenay West would say, are very urgent matters for the people in my constituency. I should like to remind the minister to provide post office facilities at Fort Nelson and Taylor.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Cariboo and I are departing to attend the commonwealth parliamentary conference. He did not take the time I expected he would in discussing the estimates for the Department of Public Works. The fact he mentioned such matters as the Alaska highway and the removal of the charges for travel on the trans-Canada highway through federal parks, indicates how widespread the subject matters are that can be discussed at this time. One could contrast his remarks with the fairly lengthy observations to which we listened on the subject of the Montreal world fair. In so far as the Montreal world fair is concerned, I certainly wish it well. I was one of the members who spoke in support of the bill which established the Canadian corporation. However, I am not disposed at this time to enter into any detailed dis-

Supply-Public Works cussion such as was undertaken by those who spoke from the Conservative benches. Perhaps later in this discussion one of my colleagues may have something to say about it.
I should like to support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cariboo that consideration be given to the elimination of this charge for travelling on the trans-Canada highway through national parks. I know a great many people who are interested in the new through route between Calgary and Vancouver, and who are not planning to visit the park, do find this charge a bit of an imposition. In fact, we have created a toll road over part of the trans-Canada highway as a result of this arrangement in respect of our national parks.
At the outset of my remarks, I should like to say that, in some ways, I have enjoyed the approach which has been taken in the house by our new Minister of Public Works. I cannot say that I shall do my best to see he occupies that post for the next 20 years, as he indicated he might wish to do. Certainly during the time he does occupy that post, I shall do my best as a member who has a considerable interest in the activities of his department to assist him in the proper discharge of his duties. At this particular stage in our discussion, perhaps it would not be amiss if the work done in this department by the person who occupied the post of deputy minister for quite a number of years was mentioned. Those of us who had dealings over a period of time with Major General Young appreciate some of the efforts he made for us in attempting to streamline and modernize the federal Department of Public Works. I felt that that contribution of his should not go unnoted in this discussion.
While I applaud the minister for being fairly forthright in answering questions put to him across the floor, I must admit I was somewhat disappointed that in his opening statement he did not outline in more detail his concept of the role his department should be playing on the Canadian scene. He indicated that a year from now, if he is still occupying that portfolio, he will have more to say than he said tonight. This brought home to me very obviously that the famous 60 days of decision had not reached into the operations of the Department of Public Works, and perhaps in view of what happened in connection with one or two other ministers who were in the forefront during those 60 days, the minister may have been wise not to emphasize that type of role. Nevertheless I think it would have been useful to have had some statement from him

regarding his department's activities in the future.
He did mention that we could anticipate some increase in the estimates for his department next year; but if his idea of a heavy increase does not extend much further than the suggestions he made tonight when he was outlining the additions to and deletions from the program of his department, then his concept of the role of his department leaves a great deal to be desired.
I notice, in the most recent annual report of the department, that for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1962, which of course was transmitted to us under the signature of the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, a former minister, it shows the 1961-62 program of expenditures was somewhat smaller than that of the preceding year. The figures were $174,256,000 in 1961-62 as compared with $190,842,000 for the fiscal year 1960-61. Compared with the figures which the minister gave tonight, and taking into account his deletions and additions, I make the figure for this year $172,300,000, an increase of $6.3 million over last year; and considering that our population is growing year by year, this leaves us a number of millions of dollars behind the expenditure for the fiscal year 1960-61.
This suggests that the government has not as yet given any indication that it is doing something about the former Conservative so-called austerity program in the field of operations of the Department of Public Works. This is a serious lack in the policies of the government, and should be remedied.
I feel the concept of a federal department of public works should be something more than what is referred to in the last annual report, which as I said was issued under the Conservative regime, as "a construction agency for the federal government." In my view, and I think I can say in the view of the New Democratic party, this department should be an economic instrument, something which will be an active agency spearheading the economic growth of Canada; something that will act in concert with the general level of industrial and other economic activity to ensure that Canada continues to move forward at a steady pace from year to year, and on a scale commensurate with taking up the slack which exists today, and has existed over a number of years, in the field of employment. That is the sort of concept which was completely lacking in anything the minister said tonight when introducing these estimates.
I hope that between now and this time next year he will give some consideration to spearheading that kind of role for his department. If he wants to remain Minister of Public Works for the next 20 years I can think of no

better way in which he might achieve that objective than to put his department in the forefront of activities of the federal government, instead of allowing it to continue as it has been, as a sort of caretaker, back door operation. In that way it could initiate projects which I and a lot of my constituents feel it should tackle.
I can only assume that the situation which was so evident in my constituency as a result of the so-called austerity program, was something which appeared all across Canada. Even in the operations of the harbours and rivers engineering branch of the department, projects in British Columbia were slashed to a point beyond all recognition; and I would point out that even before this slashing took place there was a crying need for the early construction of many projects and the provision of many public services up and down the coastal area of British Columbia.
I shall not outline them all tonight as the minister has been getting letters from me giving the details. However I mention them for two reasons. The first is that even within the present very limited concept of the operations of the department, the government has not taken any step to restore the level of public works to what it was in 1960-61. Second, because the government has not done this, it clearly indicates that the minister is not proposing an active, dynamic role for the functioning of his department which, on the one hand, will provide the kind of public services and facilities that the people of Canada need, and on the other hand and correlated with it, operate in our economy as something to create a balance between needs and employment. By operating in that way it could bring an end to the scourge of unemployment, to which hon. members have made reference, but without providing any practical suggestions for achieving it.
Having read this last annual report put out under the signature of the Hon. E. Davie Fulton, it struck me as rather strange that those who spoke on behalf of the Conservative party carried on at such length, talking about programs of slum clearance and other projects which had not been undertaken. I am quite willing to concede that the new minister has not had time to initiate projects along those lines which, according to the hon. members who have spoken, were not undertaken in their constituencies during the previous regime. But I had hoped the minister would have given us some indication tonight that he had plans to put an end to the state of affairs which does exist, and on this I agree with other hon. members.
Supply-Public Works The hon. member for Cariboo mentioned the trans-Canada highway. There are one or two matters I would like to deal with in that connection and one or two questions I would like to raise with the minister. I wish to refer briefly, Mr. Chairman, to the last annual trans-Canada highway report. Apparently it came out a little later than the report of the department, because it bears the name of the present Minister of Public Works. On page 2 of the report I find these words:
In I960 it was again apparent that the completion of the highway would not be possible in some provinces during the construction period provided for in the existing agreements. A third amendment of the act in May, 1960 extended the construction period to December 31, 1963, and increased the aggregate amount that may be contributed by Canada to $400 million.
As I understand it, that is the position of the Trans-Canada Highway Act at the present time; in other words, the termination of the trans-Canada highway agreement will soon be reached, namely on December 31 of the current year. Yet on the next page of the report I find some detail as to the state of the trans-Canada highway at the time the report was prepared. It says:
Considerable construction still remains to be done in the province of Newfoundland. There appears to be little possibility of construction being completed on the entire Newfoundland mileage before the end of the construction period provided for in the present agreements.
That is, by December 31 of this year:
The province of Quebec has made an auspicious start on the construction of its section of the highway. Continuation of the work on a large scale during the 1962 and 1963 construction seasons will insure the completion of a high percentage of the highway mileage during these years. It is, however, unlikely that the construction of the entire mileage across the province can be completed before the termination date of the agreement.
The province of Ontario is continuing with the work of reconstructing substandard sections of the highway. Although it appears unlikely that all substandard sections will be upgraded before December 31,	1963, there will be a continuous
paved highway across the province by that date.
Those of us who have been in the house over a period of time realize that the Trans-Canada Highway Act expiry date has been extended on more than one occasion; that the original program of completion of the first trans-Canada highway by 1956 fell by the board long ago. But I think the statements in this report do call for some clear indication from the government as to whether before the end of this year we will have some legislation brought before parliament to again extend the period of the trans-Canada highway agreements, or whether these statements have been superseded by more recent developments and the trans-Canada highway will in fact be completed before the end of this year.

I think all of us agree that the construction of the first trans-Canada highway was a most important and valuable undertaking in this country. I think it is one of the things which will in future years, and more and more as the years go on, tend to assist the Canadian people from one end of this country to another to get to know one another better.
I think perhaps no single construction project may in the long run tend to diminish some of the tensions that exist at the present time within the Canadian confederation more than the increasing use that will be made of this trans-Canada highway by travel-conscious Canadians. Therefore I would hope there is no question that this project will be continued to completion and that the necessary action will be taken by the government to achieve this end.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps my hon. friend would permit me to make an observation at this point. In the supplementary estimates D, vote 178d-which vote is being added to the present estimates of my department-the hon. member will see that we are asking the house to extend the termination date of the Trans-Canada Highway Act from December 31, 1963, to December 31, 1967.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the minister to say that there is an item of increased money in a supplementary estimate. Does that mean the construction program is to be accelerated so that the highway will be physically completed by that vote? Does he mean that the extension of this agreement can be achieved by the voting of an item in the estimates rather than by the introduction of an amending bill?
If my hon. friend would permit me to say this, Mr. Chairman, the effect of voting item 178d-
One dollar.
-will be to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act, which would terminate on December 31, 1963.
It is a standard procedure; a $1 open door.

I thank the minister for his explanation, but I find it a little puzzling that an act can be amended by the simple expediency of a vote in the estimates. However, that is the kind of question which, if it is to be discussed any further, I would prefer to have dealt with by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. It seems to me, offhand, to be a rather peculiar approach, and I do not think it was the one taken previously when I was in the house and the termination date was extended.

Mr. Chairman, I have given the hon. member this information in order that he may be aware of the fact that we want to extend the Trans-Canada Highway Act beyond December 31, 1963. As I understood his remarks, the hon. member was inquiring as to what we were doing about this matter. I would suggest that when we reach this item we can discuss the way it will be done.
The hon. member will be away.

I wish to thank the minister for giving the committee, and myself in particular, this information at this time, Mr. Chairman, because I thought it was a matter that should be clarified and, in my view, the sooner the better. I am certainly happy the minister has indicated that the intention of the government is to make the necessary extension and provide the necessary financing required for the completion of the highway, because this enables me to go on to some other remarks that I wish to make.
I feel that the time has come when both this house and the minister should be looking beyond the completion of the first trans-Canada highway. I do hope that before the discussion of these estimates is concluded there can be an opportunity for some fairly full discussion of this whole matter. I should merely like to state briefly at this time that I feel the completion of the trans-Canada highway should be the beginning of a much broader concept of highway development in Canada. I should also like to say that I feel the program of highway development should be increasingly geared to the concept of a national transport policy which would include, in the consideration of the planning involved, our railway system, our air lines system and our coastal and inland water transportation system, so that the planning and development done would produce unified and co-ordinated transportation facilities for the use of the Canadian people as individuals and for commercial purposes. I recall that a number of years ago, under the administration of the previous Liberal government, action was taken in this house to relinquish federal jurisdiction over interprovincial trucking, I felt at that time, and I still feel, that that was a retrograde step as far as the development of an adequate transportation system and policy in Canada is concerned. I feel it was probably done at that time because the government of the day had not thought out the implication of highway building as a national need in the context of the current situation. I hope that we can push forward to the point where the resources of the whole nation will be behind

the development of a proper national highways program. I think that is certainly one of the areas of activity in which the people who live in the great country to the south of us have given us an example of what can be done. Within the limits of our smaller population and developed resources I think that Canada should long since have followed in the footsteps of that sort of program in a much more adequate way than we have in the undertaking of the single trans-Canada highway program.
I could relate this situation with respect to a highway policy to some of the things I have run into in the course of my travels in the coastal areas of British Columbia. One of the things in which I think the federal government has failed, be it a Liberal or Conservative administration, is in what in common parlance today is called doing a selling job of the highway program. I think this is because there has been this lack of a concept of a real national transportation policy which would have a unifying effect on the Canadian nation. The result of it, certainly in British Columbia, has been that, to put it bluntly, nearly all the credit for the building of the trans-Canada highway has been taken by the provincial administration. That situation may or may not prevail in other provinces to a greater or lesser degree, but we happen to have a minister of highways in British Columbia who is pretty fond of blowing his own horn and giving the impression that he is the only one in the whole country who knows anything about building highways. Because of the lack of understanding among the Canadian people, through lack of initiative by the Canadian government, of a national highway program, it has been possible for a great deal of misrepresentation of the situation to take place.
I think that nowhere has this been more evident than in the northern part of Vancouver island, where there has been a crying need for highway development for a number of years. I find there has been created there quite successfully and skilfully, the impression that the reason there is no highway through to the north end of Vancouver island is because the federal government decided that it would not build a trans-Canada highway to Cape Scott which is the northern tip of the island. I have had to waste a lot of my time trying to explain to people that basically the route of the trans-Canada highway was selected by the provincial authorities, and that it was the government of British Columbia which decided that the trans-Canada highway should run on Vancouver island from Nanaimo south to the city of Victoria.
Supply-Public Works But that does not mean that there is no need for federal participation in a highway program, and this is one of the areas where a broad national policy could very well come into play.
