I was just about to say that the coastal area of British Columbia is one of the parts of Canada where the broader concept of a highway building program-and because it is a sea coast area, in conjunction with other means of transport-could very well come into play. I know that this same crying need exists in other parts of the country as well. I have listened to a lot of discussion about the need for the Yellowhead route through from Edmonton to the city of Prince Rupert, which is in the constitutency of my hon. friend from Skeena. One could go on, I am sure, and enumerate situations right across the country where it would be in the national interest that we develop this broader national highway concept.
There is only one other matter I wish to raise at this point. I should like some clarification from the minister before the estimates are concluded as to what the thinking of the present government is in respect to the establishment of federal buildings. I know that during the years I was out of the house a program was initiated to build federal buildings for the use of the Post Office Department in many of the smaller communities, where such had not been the case in previous years. I should like to know whether it is the intention of the present minister and his government to continue with that policy. I suppose that in most constituencies in Canada, outside of the large urban areas, this is quite an important question. I know of one or two communities in my constituency, such as Port Hardy for example, where there is urgent need of better postal facilities, and where the department has previously acquired property which is not presently, or as far as I know, within the plans of the department for use for the erection of such a building. I think it is important that this matter should be clearly stated as a matter of policy on the part of the present government, in view of the fact that in this particular area there was undoubtedly a change of policy by the former

Supply-Public Works Conservative government in relation to the policy pursued by the previous Liberal administration.
With that, Mr. Chairman, I will conclude my remarks at this stage of the discussion.

The Department of Public Works is, of course, familiar with the district of St. John's West, and the district of St. John's West with the Department of Public Works. I did not think I could let this opportunity pass without making a few comments, while the estimates of the department were before us, because this particular department has a great role to play not only in the district of St. John's West but in all of Newfoundland.
The previous speaker suggested that the federal government had perhaps not done a good selling job vis-a-vis the credit involved in the construction of the trans-Canada highway. I might say that until a few months ago this was an academic question in Newfoundland because the federal government was paying 50 per cent of the cost, and while this arrangement existed it would be some time before Newfoundland would ever enjoy this highway. We are pleased to note that the new government has taken action in this direction and we hope that in the near future the trans-Canada highway will be completed.
However, the role of this department as far as Newfoundland is concerned, and as far as St. John's West is concerned, means more than the building of the trans-Canada highway. I thought there was a good deal of merit in some of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni regarding the attitude, or philosophy, or approach he would like to see taken by the Department of Public Works. I would like to take this opportunity of saying that over the past year I have had considerable contact with the department and its officials both in St. John's and in Ottawa and from my encounters with them, I am pleased to say, it seems clear that they do have these things at heart. Although at times we might disagree about some of the things they may be doing, all in all the relationship has been satisfactory.
I think it would be wrong at this time to enter upon a debate on this issue, but we take note of the fact that the estimates before the committee, those compiled by the previous administration, were, unfortunately, affected by the austerity program. Hon. members from British Columbia recalled that their province suffered as a result of that program and the same is true, I suppose, of all ten provinces. It is certainly true of Newfoundland.
The Department of Public Works has a role to play in the economic growth of the

province I am happy to represent. Decisions to undertake harbour improvements such as the building of wharves or breakwaters in fishing communities undoubtedly add to the wealth of those communities and make it easier for the fishermen to fish. Over the past 14 years a number of noteworthy improvements have been made. We were encouraged by the remarks the minister made in opening this discussion. What is of great importance to us is that in future estimates a larger amount of money should be made available for such projects as I have mentioned. Expenditure of this sort could be justified on many grounds.
I might say that in the district of St. John's West, which is, in fact, two thirds an urban riding, there are 61 or 62 communities. I tried to total them up before rising to speak. There are 61 or 62 harbours in the district. The population in some of these places is small but it is clear that here we find the basic economy of Newfoundland, because these people must make their living from the sea. A problem has arisen, inasmuch as in some of these smaller communities extensive harbour improvements or other public works are required at a cost which it is difficult to justify on purely economic grounds. Some effort has been made in the past-and I hope it may continue-to centralize these projects, that is to say, to provide facilities in one community which would be of benefit to neighbouring communities. Certainly, a great many people have advocated such an approach, and it is a laudable approach; but considerable difficulty is involved because when people have made their homes for generations in these smaller communities there are important sociological aspects to be considered, quite apart from the financial burdens on individuals who must go further before they can begin their work. My own impression is that efforts on the part of the government to proceed with centralized projects of this kind would meet with small progress.
The situation in Newfoundland is unique in many respects, particularly since our people are scattered along 6,000 miles of coast line in some thousand or more communities. They have settled in these communities and made a living there with varying degrees of success. One might say on seeing some of these communities: Why don't they move somewhere else? But when you enter the community and see the lives the people lead you would perhaps be reluctant to change them. Sometimes, in these smaller communities where there are fewer facilities than in many of the larger ports, the people are more successful in the fishing. The fact that

there may be only 50 fishermen does not particularly bother them. These people who engage in the fishing industry expect the government to pay some attention to their problems.
We have heard a great deal of discussion about the world fair in Montreal. It is difficult for people who want $10,000 or $12,000 to build a wharf which would be of immense value to them to read, with equanimity, that $18 million was voted for this, and $22 million for that. We may put forward all the economic arguments in the world, but in the last analysis, it is difficult to explain. But I do hope that the minister and the department are aware of this and I feel confident that they are. As I say, I am not debating the merits or demerits now, because this type of austerity program is over. However, I thought it was necessary to draw to the attention of the house and the minister-perhaps it did not need to be drawn to the minister's attention-the fact that this did set back the development of Newfoundland considerably, because it is only economically possible for the Department of Public Works to carry out two, three or four listed projects in a given area or along a good portion of the coast in one year. When we have had a year or two years in which the normal amount of spending on these smaller public works projects has been cut it sets back the economy, and at this time, with the renewed interest in the fisheries and with the interest of the Minister of Fisheries in the development of a national fishery policy, the Department of Public Works has a very important role to play in the development of the fishery in Newfoundland.
In essence I suppose what the situation really boils down to is that what is needed is a considerable increase in spending. There are those, of course, in the house who object for some reason or other and who feel that at this time we cannot spend too much on works of this type. However, I come back to the point raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that if we can look at these expenditures as economic investments in the community and in the province they can be justified. From my contacts with the officials of the department and the minister, I know they are very much aware of the situation. In my view the important need is that the government as a whole and the members of the House of Commons, who must vote on the estimates of this department, should be aware of the great role that this department can play, and that all of us realize that this sort of spending can help, particularly in ridings such as those represented by the two members from British Columbia who have spoken, and the ridings of Newfoundland 28902-5-241
Supply-Public Works where there are Canadians making their living in small communities. It is an investment in those people and in those communities because it can help them to improve their lot.
We can talk too much about centralization, because what kind of a country would Canada be if everybody lived in a city with approximately 100,000 people? We would all start to look alike, talk alike and walk alike and I think it would be a very boring country. One of the tremendous attractions of Canada is that it is a big country with many little communities scattered throughout the land, and while this may cause many problems for us I think we must recognize that if we develop these rural communities they will respond. Indeed, one of the responses may well be that some of those living in exceptionally small communities may realize that by going to a little larger community they may be able to improve their lot in life. If we show our willingness to develop I think they will cooperate with us. A thought has just occurred to me, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear.

I should say that a new thought has occurred to me, and it is one that required a little prompting before it did occur. I wish to note the fact that, now that we are discussing the nation's business, and now that I am trying to make clear the case of Newfoundland, there is not one member of the creditistes group present in the house to show any interest in my problems and the problems of the many people in the small communities of Newfoundland. I will certainly convey that fact to my friends in Newfoundland.
We have our problems too and they are many and varied. We are patient and we listen to other people's problems, and I hope we are not inflicting ourselves on you too much if as new Canadians we bring our problems forward. There are those who are not in the Social Credit group, under the leadership of the hon. member for Villeneuve, who are not interested in the problems of Newfoundland. There are others in other groups in the house who have made remarks indicating that they have little knowledge of our problems and do not really care. We know these things; but in life that has to be our lot one way or another, and we are prepared to cope with it.
As I say, I feel there must be an increase in the estimates of this department because in my view the economic effects thereof are sufficient justification. In my own district

Supply-Public Works there are four or five major harbour developments that are necessary. I know the department is very much aware of them and I hope that in the next few years these particularly important projects will be undertaken. I believe the net result will be a general improvement.
There are two particular votes that will come up later about which I should like to comment in passing, the dredging vote and the miscellaneous vote. In my opinion both of these votes should be increased because I find there is some difficulty from time to time in being able to get all the dredging done I should like to see done in the riding of St. John's West. The lack of this dredging causes great inconvenience to many of the fishermen in these small rural communities.
I have already drawn it to the attention of the minister but I should like to reiterate that if we increase the miscellaneous vote many of these small jobs that are not listed items could be performed and great progress could be made. I think it is unfortunate we had to have an austerity program because it hurt my district as it did many others.
It is over now.
The minister says it is over now. This is good news for St. John's West and Newfoundland generally.
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity of putting a few questions and thoughts before the Minister of Public Works in relation to the highway development program.
Louder.
Are you hearing me over there, or was that a facetious remark? If so, I shall be glad to accommodate you.
Be careful, we will not sell your wheat.

We are not talking about wheat; we are talking about highways. The hon. member's facetious remark about wheat will be dealt with in due course when the estimates having to do with wheat and the Department of Agriculture are before the house.
To return to the subject of highways and highway development, a subject dear to my heart and to the hearts of the people I represent, we in the Crowsnest pass and that area extending from Medicine Hat through Pincher Creek, Cowley, Blairmore, Hillcrest, Coleman, Fernie and Nelson to Vancouver have been asking that No. 3 highway be made an alternate trans-Canada highway to No. 1. I am glad to see that the hon. member for Kootenay East is prepared to support me.

He represents the constituency to the west of me, and if there is one thing that the people are saying to him and also to me it is that the time is long past that the parliament of Canada should co-operate with the provinces to make highway No. 3 an alternate trans-Canada highway. I hope the Minister of Public Works is listening to me, because I am wondering why in the estimates now before us there is a $10 million cut in the highway appropriation to the provinces. I should like to ask the minister if, as a result of this $10 million cut, he was forced to forgo any consideration of a contribution towards making this No. 3 highway an alternative route to No. 1. What we need in southern Alberta and southern British Columbia is an all-weather highway, one which can be travelled in any month of the year without fear of being blocked by snowfalls or ice conditions. The only western route on which one can be sure of that is the one which I have described, branching off through Medicine Hat and going west through the Crowsnest pass.
Many years ago the people of the Crowsnest pass area felt that the No. 1 highway should go through the Crowsnest pass, through Nelson and on to Vancouver. However, vested interests in Calgary and Banff were successful in having the present route established. We have no quarrel with that. However, we do say that the alternative southern route should be established. I should like the Minister of Public Works, who is responsible for highways, to go out and visit the area. I shall be glad at any time to take him over that route, and I am sure the hon. member for Kootenay East would join with me. We would give him a first hand glimpse of that part of the country and give him an idea of the merit of my suggestion at this time.
This road has been black-topped most of the way by the provincial departments of highways. However, in order to bring the road up to federal standards, and in order to take care of the tourist traffic in that area, other work would be necessary. The tourist traffic is important to the people of that area, so it is important that an all-weather road be established for travellers who wish to go from the prairie provinces to Vancouver during the winter or any time of year, on business or for pleasure.
If I might finish my original thought, I should like the Minister of Public Works to visit that area. I know that he is new at his job and he cannot be expected to know everything about every comer of the country. Has the minister ever been to the west to familiarize himself with the conditions that exist there? He is nodding his head, indicating

that he has. I shall, therefore, expect action from him to make this No. 3 highway an alternate route for the people of that area. The chamber of commerce of the Crowsnest pass area has been able recently to obtain from the provincial government a promise to develop a provincial park in the area which has the greatest tourist attractions of any part of Canada. There is the Frank Slide, and beautiful scenery including Crowsnest mountain, and many other attractions in that area.
I notice that there has been $10 million cut from the appropriation and I am wondering if this government wants to curtail these important developments, or are they in financial difficulties and trying to balance their budget by making these cuts? I contend that this is no time to be giving consideration to reduction when such important matters for employment as the development of our highway system are being considered. A cut of $10 million at this time is quite unreasonable.
In closing, I want to say that the second largest industry in the Dominion of Canada is the tourist industry. We should like the Minister of Public Works to give earnest consideration to highway No. 3. When he is travelling in the west with us, I should like him to look at another proposed road from this route which goes through Red Rock canyon in Waterton Lakes park to Coleman in Crowsnest pass. A certain amount of work has been done on this route, but it has not been completed. We should like to have the minister come out and familiarize himself with this project. Above all, we shall look for action just as soon as possible and hope that construction will begin next summer.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. A few minutes ago the hon. member for St. John's West was belabouring the committee because some members were absent tonight. He said they were not giving attention to the problems of Newfoundland. Yet, no sooner had he finished speaking than he left the chamber and he has remained absent since.

I am just going to take two or three minutes of the committee's time to lay before it a rather personal feeling, a rather personal belief. Before I came to this parliament I was engaged in the business of constructing buildings. I have, therefore, some knowledge of the cost of structures. In pursuing that business, I built a number of buildings, some of which were of magnificent design and were inexpensive in costs, while others were very costly buildings but were atrocious. In travelling across the country, I have seen a number of public buildings of fine design. I have seen also some public buildings that are atrocious.

Supply-Public Works
I understand that there are expenditures which are not covered by these estimates, but are located elsewhere in the estimates, which are devoted to trying to foster good design in all types of art. It seems to me that in the Department of Public Works we have an opportunity to couple together the business of providing accommodation with the ideal of leaving behind examples of good design. It seems to me that this is not only an opportunity for the department, but more than that, I consider it an obligation of the department. The structures we build today are going to be here long after many of us have gone. This will not happen accidentally. It will only happen if there is a conscious awareness on the part of the minister and his department that they have a dual responsibility.
I should like, therefore, to take this opportunity to urge the minister to impress upon his department the fact that when they create a structure they are creating more than just accommodation for people or a place to work. They are creating structures that are going to influence the environments in which they are located. I think the opportunity and Obligation is there to make that influence a good one. I hope the minister and the department will be aware of this, will stress it, and so will leave in our communities structures for the people that come after us that are worthy examples of the best of our age.

Like the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I will be absent from the house for some time and I would like to make one or two remarks tonight about some items that appear in the estimates of the Department of Public Works. I would remind the committee that the house does review the estimates of the national capital commission as part of the estimates of the Department of Public Works, and I am particularly anxious to make one or two comments on the program of capital development.
On page 466 of the estimates the accounting of the loans for the development of the national capital region is given, and there is a substantial improvement in the vote here. In particular this represents a program of development of the Le Breton flats area as part of a complex of government structures and over-all planning.
I also call the attention of the committee to the program for the acquisition of the green belt, which was initiated some years ago. It is being continued and I hope it will be completed soon. The officials responsible for the development of these programs have operated very closely in co-operation with the respective municipal authorities in the different municipalities involved, and I think there

Supply-Public Works has been very little criticism of the over-all programs. A great deal is being done here that the national capital and those who take part in the life of the national capital can justifiably praise.
The program of development of the green belt is a long term one, and I hope that within the next year it will be possible to complete, or substantially complete, the acquisition of a number of properties where there have been difficulties in arriving at agreement. The over-all program is one that is much to be commended.
I would also like to refer to the vote for development of the national capital area. This shows an increase of something in excess of $3 million in the building program, and in many cases this has been long overdue. Those who visit our national capital and look at temporary structures that were erected, in some cases over 20 years ago, recognize this is a program which has to be accelerated. In spite of the difficult circumstances of the present budget a great deal is being done in this connection.
One matter about which I, as a local representative, am very pleased, is the approach which the minister himself has shown in the development of a number of major projects in the area. For example I am thinking of the general assurances which the city of Ottawa recently received from the government. I am also thinking of the proposed Heron road-Base Line road bridge, which is very necessary for the complete development of the complex of government buildings at Confederation heights. This is one project which is of very great importance to the area which I represent, and it is a project which should have been resolved long before now. I give full marks to the minister for facing the problem squarely and making forthright recommendations which give the municipal authorities a basis on which to proceed. I might add that the package is much bigger than that, and includes the Smyth road bridge and some assistance for the overpass structure.
The minister has provided some general outline of policy which the municipal authorities can count on in future years in planning an orderly development of their municipal public works as part of a national capital program. This is a great step forward, and on behalf of a number of people who have been associated with these matters, I wish to express their thanks for the appreciation, sympathy and understanding which the minister has shown in these projects. I know the municipal authorities concerned will recognize a considerable improvement in the situation over that which prevailed previously.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a question of privilege. It has been brought to my attention that some hon. member commented on my absence from the chamber. I was on the phone talking to a friend of mine in Quebec and he assured me that, although there were no members of the group under the leadership of the hon. member for Ville-neuve showing an interest in the province of Newfoundland, that did not mean there were many Quebecers who were not interested in my province's problems. That explains my brief absence from the chamber.

In my opening remarks may I say that the minister will be immeasurably assisted in his duties this year in having recently been fortunate in the appointment of his new deputy minister, who worked with me for a brief period when I was with the Department of Veterans Affairs. Having said that, I now come to deal with the estimates under discussion.
The usual aim of the debate on the estimates of the Department of Public Works is to encourage the minister to spend more money. That may be correct, provided it is directed towards the provision of useful projects within the constituencies represented by hon. members, and also on a general basis; but I do think there comes a time when we must assess the whole question of the provision of public buildings to see if we are not getting to the point where we are establishing a series of monuments of bricks and mortar to the memory of a series of successive ministers.
I feel that for the size of our nation, and with the expansion which has taken place in the post-war years, we have reached a point in the provision of government capital structures that will be sufficient for our needs for many years to come. It is true there is a great deal of replacement, particularly in some of the smaller towns and villages, where postal facilities and other types of smaller buildings must be renewed or enlarged. However, when it comes to the question of great, large buildings, we find that from one end of the country to the other there is a decreasing need for the provision of these great monuments, particularly at a cost to the crown.
I have been wondering just how intense a study has been made of lease-backs by the crown, where buildings are put up by interested individuals to the specifications of the crown or the principal tenants, and then leased back over a period of years. I wonder whether this would not be a less expensive way of providing the crown in Canada with

its necessary public buildings. I am not speaking of hospitals, but of offices.
I think there might be introduced a degree of flexibility into our system of property holdings. This degree of flexibility does not exist at present. I am sure some study has been made of it but I would be interested to knew if a really intensive study has been made and what has been the result. This could apply to other government departments that own buildings. While I am dealing with the question of large government buildings, Mr. Chairman, I would bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I am not aware of the immediate policy of his department with regard to the provision of really modern buildings with proper facilities, including air conditioning, but this is a point that deserves serious consideration. Some people may say air conditioning is a frill, but I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and through you to the minister, that in a city such as Ottawa, which in the summer time has a climatic condition that very often leads heads of departments to dismiss their staffs early in the day, or where staffs are only operating at 65 per cent or 75 per cent efficiency, to ignore this question of installing air conditioning in government buildings is cheese-paring. It is more than cheese-paring: it is a wrong policy not to provide this facility. These buildings should be provided with general air conditioning.
It is true that the minister is bound by certain treasury regulations in this regard, but surely he can bring his influence to bear on this problem and do something about it. If other ministers in the chamber also hear these words I would ask them to also consider this matter. It is all very well for the minister, who may introduce air conditioning into his office, in the office of his deputy minister and down to a certain level; but the ordinary working staff should be given equal consideration in this respect. We have in this city temporary buildings that will continue to be occupied for another 10 or 15 years, and they are actually hells in which to work during the summertime. These temporary buildings are costly to maintain. In wintertime they are inefficiently heated. There is no means of controlling the climatic conditions which prevail in this city. I am sure that in the long run we would obtain a much greater return per employee in the way of more efficient work and less absenteeism as a result of sickness if facilities were provided which would to some extent offset the climatic conditions which prevail here.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, it has been beyond my comprehension that we have continued
Supply-Public Works with this sort of prehistoric policy for so many years. We know that commercial firms in cities such as Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto instal either a complete air conditioning system or modified air conditioning in their buildings. Why do they do it? They do it because they realize it is not just a question of personal comfort but it brings a greater return in work efficiency on the part of their employees. This is not the first time I have spoken about this matter. Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, one of the reasons I have not much hair on the top of my head is that I have been butting it against a blank wall in this regard. But I will come back to this plea time and time again. I will leave the matter there, Mr. Chairman.
I would refer to another matter about which I have spoken a number of times and which was instituted a couple of years ago. I would like the minister to give us an estimate of how it has worked out. I refer to the requirement of time and material payment bonds on major contracts. There have been many unhappy experiences in this regard, particularly in the Department of Transport -I will not deal with the particular instance -and if there had been time and material payment bonds not only would we have had a faster completion of jobs but a great many subcontractors and suppliers, who in some cases went into bankruptcy because of incompletion of a contract or because of improper operation on the part of the prime contractor, would have been paid.
A great deal has been said about a second trans-Canada route. Some people advocate one route, others advocate another. We would like to know from the minister what progress has been made with respect to the conference that he indicated he was convening, or trying to convene, with the various ministers of highways of the provinces with regard to a national highways system. Whether it be known by the name of confederation routes or whether the highways be primarily north and south routes, it seems to me we must evolve a national highway policy as part of a national transportation policy. This will take a great deal of negotiation and I know the banks and certain people will bristle when I say this, but I am of the opinion that this is one of the problems we must not only face, but solve, before we can achieve ultimate development in this country.
I have another matter to which I would draw the attention of the minister. I ask him whether he has available the information that his colleagues the Minister of Labour, and the Secretary of State, and himself, were asked to provide last July when the house

Supply-Public Works was asked to pass supplementary estimates "C" under which an item of the Department of Finance, No. 50b, was to be increased by some $7 million. This item concerned projects that were on the shelf and were to be accelerated. They were small projects which would assist in providing employment in the winter. The minister should now have the information on this question. If these projects are not well on the way or on the point of starting, they will not be of any use in this program.
The last matter to which I wish to refer, Mr. Chairman, in these brief opening remarks is the question of the national war memorial on Nepean point. I ask the minister to give us the reasons for there having been a reversal of the twice announced decision within the last year with regard to this question. There may be some technical reason which the minister may be able to advance to explain this. I do not think his colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs would have been a willing party to such a decision. I am not going to advert to any division of cabinet in this regard, but knowing something of the background of this project, and having participated last February in a renewal of the decision that had been reached by the administration formed by my hon. friends opposite in 1956, I believe, or thereabouts, that this was going to be done, I would ask why there has been this reversal. I am not necessarily quarrelling with the decision and saying it is wrong, but I want to know why it was changed. Perhaps the minister will be able to furnish us with an answer. I can promise his colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs that, should he appear before the committee on veterans affairs, we will obtain complete details in this regard. Mr. Chairman, I would hope the various suggestions put forward by hon. members on this first item of the estimates of the minister's department will be given serious consideration. We will deal with other questions when we obtain complete answers from the minister.
I do not think the Minister of Public Works should operate some sort of great big pork barrel, and in all seriousness I would warn him against even the minor type of patronage, which always has a habit of being found out.
I had forgotten to ask one question which always bothered me, and that is the formula by which the minister's staff, in consultation with post office officials, determine the size of a new post office. This formula seems to have antiquity as its main characteristic, and it is my own personal experience that, no sooner does one get a post office built according to this formula in a town which has a normal, healthy growth, than within two

years we are belabouring the minister to have an expansion because the walls are just not made of rubber and we need far more space than was initially provided, and I think at far too great a cost. With those remarks, Mr. Chairman, I will call it a day on this item.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Might I ask the hon. gentleman a question. Did he express these fine sentiments about the Department of Public Works when they built what I understand was a $14 million trade school in the Edmonton area? This was under the previous administration.

If you will learn the facts you will understand that this school was built by the province of Alberta as a result of a decision by the province of Alberta to implement part of its program. The federal government had nothing to do with it, except the provision under its program of 75 per cent of a program that applied to every other part of the country. When it comes down to it, if the hon. gentleman wishes to know other things-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: The hon. member has answered my question.

-about the constituency of Edmonton West, may I also say that almost a like amount was spent by the public within separate school boards in that constituency to provide vocational training, with the result that the constituency of Edmonton West benefited from the extension of educational facilities to the tune of almost $13 million.
Mr. Chairman, not belonging to either the Liberal or Conservative party, naturally I cannot become engaged in a conversation about pork barrels or patronage.
You do not live in Saskatchewan.

No, and I do not live in Alberta either. Thank God I am not attached to the Conservative party, as is my hon. friend from Edmonton West.
I listened with interest to the initial remarks of the Minister of Public Works, as I am sure other members of the committee did, but I regret very much that the approach he has taken is one of: Give me the money to spend this year; next year I will tell you what the policy is. It is regrettable that a new government, one which sat in opposition for some four to five years, and repented during those years for what had happened in its term of office prior thereto, is not able during the period they are in government again to come up with a simple declaratory policy with respect to the manner in which the public works department will fit within

the economy of the country and the structure of government. But perhaps all we have to do-because this is the statement of the minister-is to wait until next year to see whether or not he is able to come up with a policy with respect to the action and attitude of the public works department which differs in any way from that which has been in existence for some years now.
During the time the minister was a private member he and I, at the other end of this chamber, sat with just a few seats between us. We became friends of sorts, and I was sure that that friendship would carry over, inasmuch as he is now a minister, and that it might have some bearing on public works projects in the riding of Skeena which might be borderline projects, whether they would be instituted in one year or the next.
What about the pork barrel?

I do not want to get into the pork barrel; I just want the minister to get into British Columbia and to concern himself with northern British Columbia. Perhaps friendship of a personal nature should not be the basis on which projects of public works should be considered; in any event it has no validity in the relationship now, because the minister, as an interjection to his comrade in arms from St. John's West, said that austerity was over. We need have no worries anyway, because apparently the minister now has a bottomless barrel from which to draw sheafs of money to engage in public works projects all over the nation.
And in Newfoundland.

Yes, and in Newfoundland, there is no question about that.
I should like to relate to the minister some of the things which need to be done in northern British Columbia. To be a little parochial about it, I should like the minister to come out to that part of the country and spend some time there seeing the country, meeting the people, and seeing at first hand the situations which exist. Because as the old Chinese expression goes, one look is worth a thousand reports any day. The minister's predecessor visited the riding, but that visit coincided with an election which took place. I should like the minister to come when there is no election in the offing so that there is not any doubt as to why he is there. But in case the minister does not get the chance to come out-
I will do that.

The minister says he will go, and I certainly appreciate it because I should like to be his chauffeur by car, by boat, by
Supply-Public Works airplane, or by dog sled if necessary to get him into the various parts of the constituency so that he can see just what exists there. X have written a number of letters to the minister and his predecessor, Mr. Chairman, about this wonderful part of the country, northern British Columbia. What I should like to do, inasmuch as the minister has now agreed to visit us, is to place on record some of the things in the coastal area at which I should like him to look seriously, from the point of view of my doing some initial work on them, so that when he does come he can see these projects in process of being built.
I should like to start him off in the community of Stewart, which is at the moment a relatively small community of a few hundreds of population. It is, or will be, the southern terminus of the so-called Stewart-Cassiar road being financed partially by another department of the federal government under the so-called roads to resources program. Even though the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources said in Prince Rupert a few weeks ago that he was not going to put any more money into the Stewart-Cassiar road, if he has not already changed his mind I am sure he will on reflection. In any event, Stewart is going to be the southern terminus of that highway, and will be the most northern deep sea shipping port for the entire 400 to 500 miles of British Columbia, which is presently bounded by the Alaska Panhandle international channel.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I know the hon. member would not wish to misquote me. What I said in Prince Rupert was that under the roads to resources program the entire $7.5 million of federal funds allocated to British Columbia had been apportioned to the Stewart-Cassiar road. I recall the minister of mines told me that the $7.5 million had all been spent. This was a ten year agreement, and the money has been spent in four or five years. The hon. member asked me about further funds. I did not say we would not spend any more money on this road. I said the money allocated had been entirely spent, according to the minister of mines of British Columbia.

One thing which the minister of northern affairs should realize is that this was not a ten year agreement; it was a five year agreement. The agreement was to spend $3 million a year divided equally between the federal and provincial governments for a period of five years. That is the situation with respect to the agreement. In any event it is immaterial at this juncture. I am sure the minister, upon reflection, will realize the necessity of renegotiating the agreement or of putting up additional federal money for

Supply-Public Works this particular road, so that it can be completed, and the entire north country opened up.
Stewart, inasmuch as it will be the shipping port of this area of British Columbia once the road is built, needs serious attention on the part of the Department of Public Works with a view to the provision of adequate shipping, storage, wharf and docking facilities at the head of the Portland canal. I should like to ask the minister to consider seriously developing this port to the point where there is adequate shipping to serve the needs of this part of the country to the north of Stewart.
Next, is the Indian village of Kincolith at the mouth of the Nass river. It is true there is some responsibility involved here on the part of the Indian affairs branch. This village requires both adequate dock facilities for the steamer when it calls and some sort of roadway or board walk as far up the river as the steamer cannot get into the village. We have had some correspondence with the minister's predecessor about this from time to time. I should like him to reopen the file and take another look at this request.
At the community of Port Simpson, south from there, the department built floats a few years ago but there has been a campaign to get a breakwater built there. I understand there are plans on foot to construct such a breakwater, and if that is so the people of Port Simpson will be thankful. I hope the breakwater when it is built will be an adequate one.
Further south, running into the harbour of Prince Rupert, some dredging was done by the department a few years ago across what is known as the Metlakatla bar. We had a great deal of trouble convincing the department that it should undertake the dredging of this channel. Finally, the work was done, but the channel is silting up. What is required, I think, is redredging and the provision of a concrete structure of some sort under water to make sure there is continuous channel which does not silt up because of the tide and the wind.
There is another community along the coast, small in population, but situated in a very beautiful place. The people there are of the pioneer type deserving of more concern than has been shown them by the department in years past. I refer to the community of Oona River. It is true this would be a costly item but I suggest the department should construct a suitable harbour on the south of the river and develop a breakwater there. I should like the department to reopen its file on this matter, too, since I consider it an important one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Just about $50 million now.
The minister told us he had a bottomless barrel from which he could get all sorts of money.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Not a pork barrel. The hon. member said he did not believe in a pork barrel when he began his remarks.

The minister did not say it was a pork barrel. It is a money barrel, and I am interested in getting some money out of it to look after these much needed improvements.
There is the Indian village of Hartley Bay, an isolated place some distance from the settled community of Prince Rupert. There is a breakwater of sorts there consisting of some floating logs which are anchored and which are supposed to break up the swell and waves when a storm breaks. This community is wide open to Hecate strait and, in fact, to the whole Pacific ocean in a southeast gale, and the people who live there have a hard time trying to protect their boats. I should like the minister to look at this situation from the point of view of dredging out in the bay and establishing a suitable breakwater, so that the people of this village can get adequate protection for their fishing boats during storms, particularly in the fall and spring months.
In the Indian village of Kitamaat there is also a need to establish a breakwater. I might add that these communities are populated primarily by people engaged in the fishing industry. The problem is to find protection for the fishing boats which have to be tied up. Kitamaat is at the head of a long channel, the Douglas channel, and directly in the path of any southeast gale. There is a great need to build, at or near this village, a breakwater to protect the fishing boats of those who live in this community.
Just across the bay is the smelter city of Kitimat which was established a few years ago. Unfortunately it is almost entirely under the control of the Aluminum Company of Canada. I suggest that what the federal government must do is establish a government dock there and an assembly wharf so that Kitimat can be turned into a deep sea shipping port, perhaps a lumber assembly wharf. Some steps must be taken to serve the public need in that area; it should not be left under the control of one concern as it is now.
In the municipality of the village of Terrace, a federal building was put up a few years ago. The situation here is identical with that mentioned by the hon. member for Edmonton West a few minutes ago. The

building was too small from the day it was built and an extension is badly needed. Terrace is one of the fastest growing communities in the whole north country. The population is expanding by leaps and bounds. The facilities provided by the federal building are just not adequate to serve even the existing population. I think an intensive study must be made both of this and other work which should be undertaken there.
In Prince Rupert, in 1926, a grain elevator was built, designed with the possibility of duplication through the addition of facilities equal to those originally provided. The need for elevator space exists today even more than it did then. We are in the midst of making huge grain exports. Therefore we should take advantage of the government elevator at Prince Rupert. I understand that to double the capacity of the elevator at Prince Rupert the cost would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $1.25 a bushel of storage capacity, which would bring the total cost to $1,500,600 or $2 million. This project is necessary and we would like to see it undertaken.
In the few minutes at my disposal perhaps I can vicariously take the minister to the jewel of the north Pacific coast, the Queen Charlotte islands. Here too we have people who primarily follow the fishing industry, who have quite a large investment in fishing boats and who need breakwaters, wharves and floats adequate to serve their requirements and to protect their investment. In the area between Queen Charlotte city and the Skide-gate thousands and thousands of dollars have been invested by the people in fishing boats, and in the whole area there is not a breakwater of any sort behind which they can shelter in case of a storm. Boats have been lost regularly year after year. I know that the minister's department, before he came to office and even recently, has undertaken studies and surveys of the situation. It may be a costly project. It may be that the bottom in the inlet is not suitable for rock breakwaters. It may be it is just a lot of muck and ooze with no really solid bottom to it, but I am sure that somewhere in that area a suitable bottom and a sufficient amount of rock can be found to build a breakwater to protect the investment in fishing boats of the people who live there.
Queen Charlotte city is the site of the only hospital on the Queen Charlotte islands. It is also the site of the R.C.M.P. detachment and people use it as a communications centre and for everything else. There are no adequate wharf facilities there. There are no adequate aeroplane float facilities and there certainly is no breakwater of any sort to protect boats.
Supply-Public Works I think what is required is something more than the investigations that have been undertaken in the past.
There is also the matter of redredging Skidegate narrows which were dredged seven, eight or ten years ago. I know this project is under study by the department because I have had correspondence with the minister about it. But the study needs to be intensified because this is a most necessary public project requiring to be carried out on the Queen Charlotte islands.
The small community of Port Clements is where the road serving the MacMillan and Bloedel Powell River camp at Juskatla begins. There is a need to rebuild the wharf and the shed at the end of the wharf at Port Clements. This project has been under study by the department for three or four years but so far nothing has been done. This is a small item in the millions of dollars the minister has at his disposal and in the millions of dollars that are spent by the public works officials, but it is most necessary and vitally important to the people who live in that area and who are served by that particular wharf and shed.
Up at Masset we would like the minister to put some money into redredging what is known locally as the Delkatla slough. This was dredged a few years ago but unfortunately, because of the manner in which it was dredged, the wind has blown some of the sand back into the basin. There is also a tidewater slough behind it and every time the tide runs out it brings down silt and muck and deposits it in the Delkatla basin. We would like to have that redredged. The provincial government is at present building a causeway there. I do not know whether the Department of Public Works is participating in that project but I think it certainly should from the point of view of assuring that the basin will not resilt every time the tide runs out of the slough, and so that there will be some guarantee that when it is dredged it will stay that way.
A few years ago we were able to get the department to do some dredging at a place called Wiah point or Seven Mile point. This is the site of the Prince Rupert fisherman's co-operative fishing camp. It is a small place but it is almost the only haven along the whole north coast of the Queen Charlotte islands where these people troll for salmon. I am thankful and the fishermen are thankful for the dredging that has been done, but there are often strong northeaster winds and it is necessary to have a rock breakwater on a reef that runs out just above Wiah point.

Supply-Public Works We would like this project to be undertaken as well.
I know that there are only a few minutes left until 10.30. I have some other thoughts to express with regard to federal buildings generally within the riding, and the trans-Canada highway. I know that members generally do not like to start on a subject and after two or three minutes have to interrupt themselves and resume on another day. I do not like to do so either. If it is agreeable to the committee perhaps I could call it 10.30 now, or I could spend the next couple of minutes talking about the necessity of a second trans-Canada highway from Prince George to Prince Rupert.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that we call it 10.30?

Agreed.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Could I ask the acting house leader what the business will be for next week in so far as he can go?

On the first two days of the week we will have a supply motion. Presumably the motion having to do with concurrence in the report on the standing committee on privileges and elections will be dealt with very quickly on Monday, I hope. I am sorry that I cannot go beyond Tuesday.
At 10.30 p.m. the house adjourned, without question put.

Monday, October 21, 1963
